news.title: A.J. Brown (ankle) out at least six weeks

fp.note: Bhayshul Tuten will compete with Chris Rodriguez to be the lead back for the Jaguars in 2026. I want to bet on Tuten this year and his talent. Last year, Tuten was unfortunately robbed of the stretch run of his rookie season as he was sidelined by a finger injury. Before the injury, he was starting to make some noise. This could be the big breakout season for Tuten, who, on a per-touch basis, flashed the immense talent that I really liked when he was in college. Last season, among 55 qualifying backs, he ranked fifth in rushing success rate, 11th in missed tackle rate, and 17th in yards after contact per attempt. Rodriguez will remain a worry for Tuten at the goal line and for his overall touch count until we see his role fleshed out this season. That uncertainty makes it tough to count on Tuten as an RB2 in Week 1. He could ultimately produce like one this week, but it's tough to project that at the moment. The Browns should field a solid run defense again this season. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Cleveland allowed the 11th-lowest explosive run rate, the 12th-lowest rushing success rate, and the 11th-lowest missed tackle rate.

Christian Watson got the bag this offseason and should be considered the clear WR1 for the Green Bay Packers. Watson deserved the payday as he proved that he can handle this role last year. Last season, in Weeks 8-18, he was the WR21 in fantasy points per game with an 18.2% target share, 61.1 receiving yards per game, 2.67 yards per route run, a 23.9% first-read share, and 0.122 first downs per route run. His target share and first-read share should go up this season with Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks gone and Watson likely getting promoted into a full-time role. Last year, he was also held back by a 68% route share (56th out of 109 qualifying receivers). Jordan Love will be blitzed incessantly this week by Brian Flores, but that should work in Watson's favor. Last year, when Love was blitzed, Watson was tied for the team lead with a 26% target-per-route run rate while ranking second with a 21% first-read share and posting 2.60 yards per route run. Last year, Minny allowed the second-most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers. I expect Watson to shine in Week 1.

Rhamondre Stevenson was the Pats' lead back last year as the RB21 in fantasy points per game, and I don't see that changing in 2026. Stevenson was amazing on a per-touch basis, and he bested TreVeyon Henderson in EVERY discernible metric that I care about. Last year, Stevenson was fifth in explosive run rate, missed tackle rate, and yards after contact per attempt (per Fantasy Points Data). Stevenson also surpassed Henderson in yards per route run (1.41 vs. 0.98) and pass protection. Unless Stevenson falls off in 2026, he should remain the lead back for New England after playing at least 57% of the snaps in nine of his 14 games played in 2025. Stevenson should have a productive day, but it won't be easy sledding in the rushing department. Last year, Seattle allowed the lowest explosive run rate, the fifth-lowest rushing success rate, and had the fifth-highest stuff rate. Stevenson will have to get it done as a receiver, which he should be able to. Last year, among 52 qualifying backs, Stevenson ranked 15th in yards per route run and first in yards per target. Seattle allowed backs to "run through the air" all season, giving up the eighth-most receiving fantasy points per game, the ninth-most receiving yards, and the most receptions to the position.

Mike Evans is practicing, so I'm projecting him to be active in Week 1. Evans might be older, but he hasn't slowed down when you look at his metrics. Last year, during his seven full games played, he had a 24.4% target share, a 30.6% first-read share, and 0.116 first downs per route run. Among 109 qualifying receivers last year, those numbers would have ranked 13th-best across the board. Yes, during that sample, he had only 1.86 yards per route run and 52.6 receiving yards per game, which would have ranked 31st and 33rd among the same group of receivers, but that was more related to Baker Mayfield's inaccuracy than Evans slowing down. In his full games played, Evans had only a 70.9% catchable target rate, which among those 109 receivers would have ranked 84th. Evans' on-field production didn't match his deeper analytics and target-earning ability, as he was also second-best in separation and route win rate last season. Last year, the Rams did allow the 14th-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers, but they also added Trent McDuffie (2025: 66.7% catch rate and 93.0 passer rating) and Jaylen Watson (2025: 63.8% catch rate and 89.1 passer rating) this offseason to address this issue. If you have Evans on your team, you're likely starting him this week. Evans still has the talent to succeed in a tough matchup.

Stefon Diggs will be Terry McLaurin's running mate this season. Diggs had a strong 2025 season that proved that he has plenty left in the tank to post a strong fantasy season in 2026. Last year, he was the WR23 in fantasy points per game with only a 65.4% route share (62nd out of 109 qualifying receivers). Among 109 qualifying receivers, he was stellar on a per-route basis, ranking 22nd in target per route run rate (25%), 20th in receiving yards per game (59.6), and eighth in yards per route run (2.53) and first downs per route run (0.127). Among the same sample of receivers, he was also 28th in overall separation score, 18th in separation versus man coverage, 22nd in route win rate against man coverage, and 11th in yards per route run against both man and zone coverages. Last year in Washington's two meetings with Philly, the Eagles utilized two-high with 60.4% of their defensive snaps. Last year, against two high, Diggs had a 26% target per route run rate and 2.24 yards per route run. Those are both stellar numbers, and with the consolidated target tree in Washington, I expect Diggs to see healthy volume in Week 1. I just worry about his ceiling with this tough matchup. Last year, Philly allowed the third-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Last year, with Ben Johnson, Caleb Williams took a small step forward in his play, but it wasn't nearly as massive a step as most think. Yes, he was the QB7 in fantasy points per game while ranking 12th in rushing yards per game and 11th in rushing touchdowns among quarterbacks, but he still struggled mightily as a passer despite the fantasy production and late-game heroics. Among 38 qualifying passers, he was 22nd in yards per attempt, 30th in adjusted completion rate and highly accurate throw rate, 34th in catchable target rate, 25th in hero throw rate, and he had the tenth-highest off-target rate. Despite all of his shortcomings with accuracy, Williams should still enjoy a nice Week 1 against a pass defense that, in Weeks 12-18 last year, allowed the third-highest passing success rate and eighth-highest CPOE, while ranking 15th in yards per attempt.

Last year, as the quarterback play in Minnesota cratered, Jordan Addison had a career-worst season as the WR44 in fantasy points per game. Addison had only a 17.4% target share with 43.6 receiving yards per game, 1.53 yards per route run, a 22.1% first-read share, and 0.065 first downs per route run. None of those numbers jump off the page, but there's hope for Addison's flex value for Week 1. Since 2023, Jonathon Gannon has utilized two high at the third-highest rate (57.6%). During the same stretch of time, against two high, Addison has seen his target-per-route-run rate climb from 18% to 20% and his yards per route run increase from 1.50 to 1.85 against two high. If Kyler Murray can prove me wrong in Week 1, Addison could have a nice game. Last year, Green Bay allowed the ninth-most receiving yards per game and the fifth-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Last year, Jacory Croskey-Merritt had an up-and-down season as the RB41 in fantasy points per game. Washington didn't trust him as a passing game option, and he was in and out of the starting lineup as the team also leaned on other backs like Chris Rodriguez. He's been working on his pass pro this offseason, and the buzz out of camp is that he'll be utilized more in the passing game this season. We'll see if that comes to fruition, but it's nice to hear regardless. In 2025, Croskey-Merritt had four top-24 finishes in weekly scoring while also popping in rushing efficiency metrics. Among 49 qualifying backs, he ranked 26th in explosive run rate, 19th in yards after contact per attempt, seventh in yards per carry on zone runs, and ninth in one rushing success rate. Behind Washington's suspect offensive line, I don't know how much running room he'll find in Week 1. I'm sitting him in most leagues where I roster him. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Philly allowed the 11th-lowest rushing success rate, the 11th-fewest yards before contact per attempt, and had the ninth-best stuff rate.

injury.comment: Jacory Croskey-Merritt (groin) will play in Week 1

news.title: Jacory Croskey-Merritt (groin) will play in Week 1

fp.note: The Carolina passing attack will flow through Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker this season. Last year, when Coker was at his healthiest (quad injury early in the year) during Weeks 13-19, he was challenging Tetairoa McMillan for the top spot in Carolina's aerial attack. During that stretch, Coker had a 20% target share (McMillan 18.3%), 2.30 yards per route run (McMillan 1.78), four red zone targets (McMillan, one), and a 28.3% first-read share (McMillan 26.1%). In those six games played, Coker finished with at least 14 PPR points four times. Last year, to close the season in Weeks 17-20, Chicago leaned into single high coverage as a pass defense (58.2%). In Weeks 13-19, against single high, Coker had a 21% target-per-route run rate and 2.81 yards per route run (WOW!). Coker is a strong flex for Week 1. Last season, in Weeks 12-18, Chicago allowed the fourth-most yards per target and the fifth-most fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers.

Last year, Hunter Henry was the TE12 in fantasy points per game while setting a new career high in receiving yards (768) and finishing with the second-most receiving touchdowns in a season in his career (seven). Among 54 qualifying tight ends, he was 15th in target share, 13th in receiving yards per game, 17th in yards per route run, and 14th in first-read share and first downs per route run. I expect Hunter Henry to take a step back in the target pecking order in New England this season with A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs on the depth chart. This opening matchup isn't kind to Henry. Last year, Seattle utilized two high at the sixth-highest rate. Against two high last year, Henry had only a 16% target-per-route-run rate and 1.08 yards per route run. Add on top that Seattle held tight ends to the 14th-fewest yards per target and ranked 15th in fantasy points per opportunity, and Henry is an easy sit this week.

Over the last two seasons, Tee Higgins has been the WR13 and WR5 in fantasy points per game. Last season, with Joe Burrow under center in Weeks 14-18, Higgins had an 18.8% target share with 67.8 receiving yards per game, 2.20 yards per route run, a 25.6% first-read share, and 0.106 first downs per route run. Those are all incredibly impressive per-route metrics. For context, if Higgins had kept up that pace for an entire season with Burrow, he would have ranked 12th in receiving yards per game, 19th in yards per route run, 28th in first-read share, and 17th in first downs per route run among wideouts (minimum 200 routes). If this offense doesn't look stuck in the mud for Week 1, Higgins should get off to a nice start against a secondary that allowed the tenth-most yards per target and the 11th-most fantasy points per game to perimeter wide receivers.

injury.comment: Tee Higgins (foot) cleared for Week 1

news.title: Tee Higgins (foot) cleared for Week 1

fp.note: Quinshon Judkins had off-the-field and contract issues last year, entering his rookie season, which caused him to miss training camp and not start the season until Week 2. Once he was on the field, he was Cleveland's workhorse back until suffering an ankle and fibula fracture in Week 16. In Weeks 2-15, he was the RB26 in fantasy points per game (RB22 in expected fantasy points per game), averaging 18.7 touches and 72.8 total yards. I wasn't high on Judkins as a prospect, as his per-touch efficiency in college wasn't amazing. He didn't debunk that trend in his rookie season, either. Among 49 qualifying backs, he ranked 40th in explosive run rate, 33rd in missed tackle rate, and 26th in yards after contact per attempt. In his defense, Judkins' offensive line didn't do him any favors last season. Among those 49 backs, Judkins had the fifth-highest mark of yards after first contact, with 62.2% of his rushing yards coming after first contact, and he had the fourth-fewest yards before contact per attempt, with only Cam Skattebo, Ashton Jeanty, and Zach Charbonnet seeing less runway with the ball in their hands. With a rebuilt offensive line to run behind in 2026, hopefully Judkins has more room to run. That will be put to the test in Week 1 against a run defense that last year, in Weeks 12-18, allowed the sixth-fewest yards after contact per attempt, the seventh-lowest missed tackle rate, and the 14th-lowest EPA per rush.

Injuries crushed Jayden Daniels' 2025 season. Daniels dealt with a knee sprain, a right hamstring injury, a dislocated elbow, and an elbow sprain. Daniels still managed to flash the upside in his four full games played last year to remind people why they fell in love with him in the first place. In those four games, Daniels averaged 20.2 fantasy points per game, nine rushing attempts, and 44 yards on the ground. If he had kept up that pace all season, he would have been the QB7 in fantasy points per game and averaged the second-most rushing yards per game among quarterbacks. With all of the injuries he sustained last year, his stats are a muddied mess that are better off tossed in the trash, but for the sake of doing my due diligence among 45 qualifying quarterbacks, he ranked 42nd in highly accurate throw rate, 38th in catchable target rate, and 25th in hero throw rate. Daniels' rushing ability will have to carry his Week 1 fantasy production because he'll be under duress when dropping back to throw against one of the best pass defenses in the NFL. Last year, Philly was fifth in pressure rate while allowing the sixth-fewest yards per attempt, the second-lowest passer rating, and the third-lowest passing success rate. I hope Washington's patchwork offensive line can give him time to throw, but I have my concerns.

Michael Wilson had Grand Canyon-sized splits last year when Marvin Harrison Jr. was out of the lineup versus when he was healthy. In the eight games Harrison Jr. was active before his heel injury and was healthy, Wilson had only an 11.7% target share, 23.4 receiving yards per game, 0.72 yards per route run, and a 14.1% first-read share. That isn't remotely close to fantasy-viable production. In the games Harrison Jr. missed and during Weeks 16 & 17 (after Harrison Jr returned post heel injury), Wilson was absolutely fantastic with a 27.5% target share, 105.6 receiving yards per game, 2.79 yards per route run, and a 38.8% first-read share (23.3 PPR points per game). That is elite WR1-level production and efficiency. Unfortunately for Wilson, Harrison Jr. is healthy to begin the season, and they are both staring at a touch matchup for Week 1 against a secondary that last year allowed the 11th-fewest receiving yards per game and the fifth-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers. Sit Wilson for Week 1.

Last year, Wan'Dale Robinson had his best season to date, easily, with a true breakout campaign as the WR14 in fantasy points per game. Among 109 qualifying receivers, he ranked 11th in target share (26.8%), 15th in receiving yards per game (63.4), 28th in yards per route run (1.94), and 11th in first-read share (32.9%). A huge change for Robinson was that he wasn't just a checkdown or underneath option anymore, as his aDOT rose to 8.7 and he was 21st among that sample of receivers in deep targets. We have no clue how this Tennessee target hierarchy will shake out at the top between Carnell Tate and Wan'Dale Robinson. Cam Ward's shaky preseason also tossed a wrench in the preseason hype gears, so Robinson can't be considered more than a PPR flex play for Week 1. Robinson has a nice matchup for Week 1, though. Last year, the Jets allowed the sixth-most yards per target to slot receivers while ranking 16th in fantasy points per opportunity. Jarvis Brownlee Jr. (2025: 77.3% catch rate and 108.9 passer rating) isn't a shutdown nickel corner.

Last year, Aaron Jones missed five games while dealing with hamstring, shoulder, and hip injuries. When he was active, he averaged 13.3 touches and 62.3 total yards as the RB31 in fantasy points per game. Entering his age-32 season, I don't think Jones can be expected to play a full 17 games as a workhorse back. He will likely split work with Jordan Mason this season, picking up most of the passing game usage. On early downs, his best days are behind him, as he was 32nd in explosive run rate, 43rd in missed tackle rate, and 49th in yards after contact per attempt. In the receiving game, he is still above average, ranking 26th in yards per route run and 24th in first downs per route run. Jones is only a middling flex to open the 2026 season against his former team. Last year, Green Bay allowed the sixth-lowest explosive run rate and the fifth-fewest yards after contact per attempt while ranking 15th in yards before contact per attempt and rushing success rate allowed.

Over the last three seasons, Brock Purdy has finished as the QB5, QB10, and QB6 in fantasy points per game. In his four years in the NFL, he has only once finished with a passing touchdown rate lower than 7.0%. Last year, among 38 qualifying quarterbacks, Purdy was sixth in passing yards per game, ninth in yards per attempt, 12th in highly accurate throw rate, and third in fantasy points per dropback. Last year, he didn't face the Rams as he missed time with injuries. This year, he'll have a tough matchup facing this defense. Last year, the Rams were a solid pass defense, and that's before they added Trent McDuffie, Jaylen Watson, Myles Garrett, and Aaron Donald unretired. Last year, Los Angeles allowed the 11th-fewest yards per attempt, the ninth-lowest passer rating, and the 14th-fewest fantasy points per game to quarterbacks. Purdy could still post QB1 numbers this week, but it won't be easy.

Could this be the year? Could this be it? The season that Dalton Kincaid FINALLY is a full-time player in the Buffalo offense? I hope so, but we still have to see if that's what actually happens in 2026. If Dalton Kincaid could get a near full-time route share, he would be a league winner and season-defining player at the tight end position. Last year, Kincaid was a monster on a per-route basis, leading to a TE13 finish in fantasy points per game. Last year, among 54 qualifying tight ends, Kincaid ranked FIRST in target per route run rate, yards per route run, separation score, route win rate, first downs per route run, and fantasy points per route run. The problem is that, among the same sample of 54 tight ends, he was 39th in route share (44.2%) behind Michael Mayer. Josh Allen could lean on Kincaid heavily in Week 1. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Houston allowed the seventh-most receiving fantasy points per game and the 11th-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Yes, D.K. Metcalf finished as the WR19 in fantasy points per game last year, but if you rostered him last season, you know that it wasn't nearly that glorious to trot him out in your lineup weekly. In nine of his 15 games played, he was outside the top 24 receivers in weekly scoring. Last year, among 109 qualifying receivers, Metcalf ranked 24th in target share (21.1%), 26th in receiving yards per game (56.7), 25th in yards per route run (1.98), 20th in first-read share (27.7%), and 37th in first downs per route run. Metcalf's Week 1 matchup does work in his favor, though. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Atlanta had the fourth-highest single-high rate (59.4%). Last year, against single-high, Metcalf had a robust 28% target-per-route-run rate and 2.38 yards per route run. In Weeks 12-18, Atlanta allowed the second-most fantasy points per game and the second-most receiving touchdowns to perimeter wide receivers. Metcalf should lead the way for Pittsburgh's passing attack in Week 1.

injury.comment: Ja’Marr Chase (knee) cleared for Week 1

news.title: Ja’Marr Chase (knee) cleared for Week 1

fp.note: Breece Hall had a tough time last year despite finishing as the RB20 in fantasy points per game. New York's quarterback play was dreadful, and the offense overall was a mess, which led to them ranking 29th in points per game and red zone scoring opportunities per game. The good news is that despite those factors, he ran behind an offensive line that ranked seventh in adjusted yards before contact per attempt. New York's offensive line remains largely intact while adding Dylan Parham to the mix to replace the often-injured and departed Alijah Vera-Tucker, so they could easily be a top-shelf unit in 2026. This is great news for a back that was also fourth in explosive run rate and tenth in missed tackle rate last year. The Titans added to their defensive unit this offseason with John Franklin-Myers, Keldric Faulk, and Jermaine Johnson. I expect them to again be a solid run defense that could take a step forward and be a top-12 unit. Last year, Tennessee allowed the 13th-lowest rushing success rate and missed tackle rate while ranking 15th in explosive run rate. This feels like a battle of the trenches in Week 1, and I like the Jets' offensive line to come out on top, with Hall having a solid day.

injury.comment: Hall is heading into the weekend entirely free of any injury designation ahead of the team's season opener against the Titans on Sunday. He shouldn't have any substantial limitations to his workload in this matchup, and he projects to be a high-quality fantasy asset in this game and beyond if he can stay healthy.

news.title: Breece Hall (groin) off injury report for Sunday

fp.note: I'm expecting Cam Skattebo to retain his lead back role to open the 2026 season, but we'll have to see if that is a bellcow role or just the leader of a committee backfield. The human battering ram known as Cam Skattebo made waves in his rookie season before being sidelined by a horrible ankle/fibula fracture that also ruptured his deltoid ligament in Week 8 of last season. In Weeks 2-7 as the Giants' workhorse, Skattebo averaged 19.5 touches and 96.3 total yards as the RB8 in fantasy points per game. Last season, he was stellar with his touches, ranking fourth in missed tackle rate and yards after contact per attempt, 11th in target per route run rate, eighth in yards per route run, and second in first downs per route run. Skattebo will face an uphill climb in Week 1 against a Dallas run defense that found its footing after the acquisition of Quinnen Williams last season. In Weeks 11-18 last year, Dallas allowed the fifth-lowest rushing success rate, the seventh-fewest yards after contact per attempt, and had the fourth-best stuff rate.

Luther Burden steps into a much larger workload in 2026. Last year (including the playoffs), Burden had only five games in which he played at least 53% of the snaps. In those games, he had a 15.5% target share and 61.2 receiving yards per game, which is concerning, but his per-route metrics were outstanding, with 2.30 yards per route run, a 23.6% first-read share, and 0.120 first downs per route run. There's a lot of projection for Burden's 2026 season. Last year, he was stellar overall per-route with a 26% target per route run rate (11th), 2.83 yards per route run (third), 0.117 first downs per route run (12th), and 0.56 fantasy points per route run (eighth, among all wideouts with at least 200 routes). In Week 1, Burden will face a Carolina secondary that, in Weeks 10-18, utilized single high with 56.9% of their snaps. Last season, against single high, Burden had a 27% target-per-route run rate and 3.35 yards per route run. Burden should begin the 2026 season with a bang. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Carolina allowed the ninth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

I don't want to read too much into the preseason usage for the Titans' backfield. Brian Daboll has a long history of utilizing one workhorse back in his offenses, so I'm still projecting Tony Pollard to be that guy. Could I be wrong and this is a 50/50 committee? Yep. Last year, Pollard ranked 15th in snap share, 17th in opportunity share, and 16th in weighted opportunities, but because of the putrid offensive situation he found himself in, he was only the RB29 in fantasy points per game. This can be traced to his five total touchdowns, which were a result of an offense that was 30th in points per game and 32nd in red zone scoring attempts per game, so it makes sense that he also ranked 49th in red zone touches. Pollard was still solid on a per-touch basis. Among 49 qualifying backs, he ranked 25th in explosive run rate and 22nd in yards after contact per attempt. The Jets added defensive firepower to their defensive line and linebacker room this offseason, so I project that their run defense will take another step forward in 2026. They were already a strong unit last season. Last year, New York allowed the sixth-lowest rushing success rate, the sixth-fewest yards before contact per attempt, and had the tenth-highest hit rate at or behind the line of scrimmage. Pollard is hopefully a volume play with RB2 upside in Week 1.

Last year, before losing the rest of his season to a torn ACL (Week 9), Tucker Kraft was the TE1 in fantasy points per game. In Weeks 1-8, among 33 qualifying tight ends, Kraft ranked seventh in target share (18.3%), first in receiving yards per game (67), second in yards per route run (2.71), seventh in first-read share (21.6%), and second in first downs per route run (0.121). Kraft was also a YAC gawd, leading all tight ends in yards after the catch per reception and missed tackles forced per reception. We'll see what Kraft's route share and overall snap share are in Week 1. The matchup isn't great for Kraft, but I'm not going to count him out in Week 1. Last year, Minnesota allowed the eighth-fewest yards per target and the 11th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Alec Pierce's offseason has been a wild one, with a lengthy ankle surgery recovery keeping him out of the preseason and for most of training camp. Pierce will be active in Week 1, but there's no way that I'd plug him into a fantasy lineup. He has been only a limited practice participant this week. I have no clue what his role or snap share will look like in Week 1. Pierce could be only an opportunistic deep threat in Week 1. With all of the uncertainty around his Week 1 playing time and effectiveness, he's a must-sit. Last season, Baltimore allowed the 11th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity and ranked 15th in yards per target against receivers.

news.title: Alec Pierce (heel) on snap count for Week 1

fp.note: Kyle Monangai has some deep league flex appeal for Week 1. Last year, in Weeks 10-18, Monangai led D'Andre Swift with 19 red zone rushing attempts compared to Swift's 18 while producing as the RB33 in fantasy points per game. During the same span, Monangai averaged 12.2 touches and 55.8 total yards while having a 28.8% route share. Monangai is a serviceable early down hammer for Chicago, ranking 24th in explosive run rate, 21st in rushing success rate, and 20th in yards after contact per attempt. If Monangai gets in the end zone in Week 1, he'll be a solid flex play, but if he doesn't, you'll likely be hating the fact that you played him despite the solid matchup. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Carolina allowed the 13th-most yards before contact per attempt, the ninth-highest missed tackle rate, and the seventh-most EPA per rush.

I'm curious what Makai Lemon's role will be out of the gate for Philly in 2026 after missing substantial parts of rookie camp, training camp, and the preseason. Lemon played on the perimeter with 71.4% of his snaps in his limited preseason action, but I doubt that will be the case when he's on the field with DeVonta Smith and Dontayvioin Wicks. Lemon finished a productive collegiate career ranking sixth and 12th in yards per route run, ninth and 50th in missed tackles forced, and 60th and 28th in YAC per reception over the last two seasons (per PFF). I expect Lemon to be the team's starting slot receiver to begin the season, and I wouldn't be surprised if he has a limited snap role if Philly looks to deploy 12 and 21 personnel heavily out of the gate. Lemon could have a solid fantasy day in Week 1, despite the risks that I outlined here. Washington couldn't stop slot receivers last year, allowing the seventh-highest passer rating and the most fantasy points per target to the position. Lemon is a decent flex play for Week 1.

Isaiah Likely's 2025 season was crushed by a foot injury that he sustained in the preseason. I can't honestly tell you whether he was fully healthy last season or when that occurred, if so. I'm tossing his 2025 campaign in the trash. So, let's be kind and rewind to 2024. During that season, among 57 qualifying tight ends, Likely ranked 17th in target per route run rate, tenth in yards per route run, and eighth in first downs per route run and fantasy points per route run. After signing a lucrative deal with the Giants this offseason, Likely should be their clear starting tight end and a strong part of their passing game. I expect Likely to open the season as the second option in the passing game behind only Malik Nabers. The Dallas secondary has been overhauled this offseason, but it's worth noting that in Weeks 12-18 last year, this defense allowed the fourth-most yards per target and the fifth-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends. Likely could easily be a strong TE1 in Week 1.

Baker Mayfield had a tough fall from grace in 2025 as the QB17 in fantasy points per game after a wondrous QB4 campaign in 2024. Mayfield dealt with injuries to his receiver room and his offensive line while also struggling with injuries himself. In 2025, Mayfield had a bruised and battered throwing arm while also suffering a sprained MCL/PCL, a bicep tendon strain, and left shoulder issues. Among 38 qualifying quarterbacks, he was 24th in yards per attempt, 35th in adjusted completion rate, 22nd in catchable target rate, and 11th-worst in turnover-worthy throw rate. In a contract year, I'm expecting a big bounce-back season from Mayfield if he can stay healthy all season, which I know is a big if for Mayfield with his play style. Mayfield should have a strong Week 1 performance, but I will also say that we need to throw every Cincy defensive statistic in the trash from 2025. The Bengals completely overhauled their defense this offseason with the additions of Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, Boye Mafe, Cashius Howell, Kyle Dugger, and Bryan Cook. Mayfield will be forced to chuck it this week to keep up with Cincy's high powered offense assuming that they come out firing on all cylinders and don't look like the middling version of this offense that we've seen stumble out of the gate early in the season.

Last year, Zay Flowers posted career-best marks across the board with 86 receptions, 1,211 receiving yards, and a WR12 finish in fantasy points per game. It was amazing to see for a player who also ranked eighth in target share (27.7%), 11th in receiving yards per game (71.2), seventh in yards per route run (2.61), and tenth in first-read share (33.3%). While Flowers also saw 19 deep targets last year, the big concern with him is his touchdown upside. Flowers has never had more than five receiving touchdowns in any season, and with only 11 red zone targets last year, it's tough to project a huge spike in that this season, but there could be hope with the arrival of offensive coordinator Declan Doyle. Flowers could get off to a fast start in Week 1 despite facing a talented Indy secondary. In the two games Indy had Sauce Gardner available last year, they utilized single high with 64.7% of their defensive snaps. Flowers destroyed single high last year with a 27% target-per-route run rate and 2.85 yards per route run. Despite having to face Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward for most of the game, Flowers has the talent to succeed in Week 1 with a nice stat line.

injury.comment: Flowers had been sidelined since the second quarter while attempting to work through the hamstring injury an return for head coach Jesse Minter, hauling in five of his six targets for 150 receiving yards and one touchdown on the day.

news.title: Zay Flowers (hamstring) ruled out Sunday

fp.note: D.J. Moore's stock took a tumble last year as Moore sank to WR41 in fantasy points per game. Moore had a 14.3% target share with 1.33 yards per route run, a 17.5% first-read share, and 0.063 first downs per route run. None of these numbers offer hope for 2026, but don't tune out just yet. Last year, among 109 qualifying receivers, Moore was 47th and 49th in separation score and route win rate. The numbers get even better when we look at Moore as a perimeter receiver, which he'll be asked to do more than the 65% of snaps that he played there last year. As an outside receiver last year, among the same sample of receivers, he was 36th in separation and 29th in route win rate. Moore has a tough matchup out of the gate against the Houston Texans. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, against perimeter wide receivers, they allowed the 11th-fewest fantasy points per game to receiving yards and the 14th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity. Moore should get peppered with volume, which should help him in this difficult matchup, but I'm not projecting a monster performance from him in Week 1.

Over the last two seasons, Courtland Sutton has been the unquestioned WR1 for Bo Nix and the Denver Broncos. In those seasons, he finished as the WR18 and WR24 in fantasy points per game. The arrival of Jaylen Waddle will change that this year. Sutton still can be a highly productive player in a pass-happy offense, but he'll take a backseat to Waddle. Sutton's per-route data remained solid, but it wasn't spectacular outside of his separation score and route win rate (20th, ninth). Last year, among 109 qualifying receivers, Sutton was 35th in target per route run rate, 32nd in yards per route run, and 29th in first downs per route run. We'll see how quickly the new (or throwback, depending on how you choose to view it) look Kansas City corner room can hit the ground running with Nohl Williams (2025: 52.6% catch rate and 85.0 passer rating) starting opposite Mansoor Delane (rookie) and L'Jarius Sneed (2025: 60.9% catch rate and 139.3 passer rating). Sutton is a solid flex/WR3 for Week 1 who could easily be a WR2.

Before his 2025 season was lost to a back injury, Sam LaPorta was the TE7 in fantasy points per game. The back has healed up well over the offseason. Despite the injury-shortened season, LaPorta was still one of the most explosive tight ends in the NFL on a per-route basis. Among 59 qualifying tight ends, he ranked tenth in target share (17.8%), sixth in receiving yards per game (54.3), fifth in yards per route run (2.14), and eighth in first downs per route run (0.100). LaPorta doesn't have the best matchup to open the season, but he could still get in the end zone and finish as a TE1 in Week 1. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, New Orleans allowed the ninth-fewest yards per target and the third-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Over the last two seasons, with Bucky Irving in town, Rachaad White was a more effective per-touch player, but with Irving out of the lineup last year, he proved again that he can carry the mail (although while being horribly inefficient). Last season, in Weeks 5-12, White averaged 14.6 touches and 60 total yards while seeing 71% of the snaps. During that span, White was the RB23 in fantasy points per game with a 1.2% explosive run rate, a 14% missed tackle rate, and only 1.52 yards after contact per attempt. White should be operating in a committee this season with Jacory Croskey-Merritt. Behind Washington's suspect offensive line, I don't know how much running room he'll find in Week 1. I'm sitting him in most leagues where I roster him. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Philly allowed the 11th-lowest rushing success rate, the 11th-fewest yards before contact per attempt, and had the ninth-best stuff rate.

Jayden Reed missed much of the 2025 season with a broken collarbone and surgery to repair a Jones fracture. Last year, we got only a five-game sample for Reed where he played at least 35% of the snaps. In those contests, Reed had a 21% target-per-route-run rate, 1.99 yards per route run, and 0.47 fantasy points per route run. Those are strong numbers, but the worry for Reed persists into 2026 about his inclusion in two wide receiver sets. Last year, Reed played 75% of his snaps from the slot, which is tough when Green Bay ranked 22nd in usage of 11 personnel (55.6%). Sit Reed this week. Last year, Minnesota allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target, the second-fewest receiving yards per game, and the sixth-fewest fantasy points per target to slot receivers.

Last year, Xavier Worthy finished as the WR54 in fantasy points per game with only one week as a top-24 wide receiver in weekly scoring. Last year, after returning from a shoulder injury (Weeks 4-17), he only had a 15.8% target share, 1.40 yards per route run, 40.9 receiving yards per game, a 19.5% first-read share, 0.058 first downs per route run, and 8.5 PPR points per game. Sit Worthy in Week 1 against a secondary that allowed the second-fewest yards per target and the fewest fantasy points per opportunity to wide receivers last season.

Romeo Doubs should be A.J. Brown's running mate this season. Last year, Doubs was the WR43 in fantasy points per game with five weeks in weekly scoring as a top-25 fantasy wideout while having only a 72.8% route share. Last year, among 109 qualifying wide receivers, Doubs was 36th in target per route run rate, 31st in yards per route run, 18th in first downs per route run, and 27th in fantasy points per route run. Also among those 109 receivers, Doubs was 23rd in separation and fifth in route win rate. Last year, Seattle had the sixth-highest rate of two-high (55.9%). Against two high Doubs had a strong 23% target-per-route run rate and 1.86 yards per route run. Doubs should see solid volume in Week 1, but make no mistake..this is a horrible matchup lining up against Devon Witherspoon and Josh Jobe for most of the game. Last year, Seattle allowed the fewest yards per target and the fourth-fewest fantasy points per game to perimeter wide receivers.

Matthew Stafford had arguably the best season of his NFL career last year, taking down the MVP award. Stafford finished with a career-high passing touchdown rate (7.7%) as the QB4 in fantasy points per game. It was easily his best season since his first year with the Rams, when he was the QB11 in fantasy points per game. Last year, among 38 qualifying quarterbacks, Stafford was seventh-best in yards per attempt and fantasy points per dropback, 25th in adjusted completion rate, second in hero throw rate, and 13th in catchable target rate. Stafford should have time to operate from the pocket this week. Yes, San Francisco will have an improved pass rush with Nick Bosa back (limited to three games last year) and the addition of Osa Odihizuwa, but this is still a defense that had the third-lowest pressure rate and the fewest sacks in the NFL last season. Last year, the 49ers gave up the 11th-most passing touchdowns, the tenth-highest passing success rate, and the tenth-most passing yards. Stafford should have a nice Week 1. Last year, in his two games against the 49ers, he was the QB8 and QB2 in weekly fantasy scoring with at least three passing touchdowns in each game.

Last year, before being lost to a knee injury (Weeks 1-6), Garrett Wilson was the WR10 in fantasy points per game. During that span, he commanded a 31.2% target share with 65.8 receiving yards per game, 1.92 yards per route run, a whopping 45.9% first-read share, and 0.087 first downs per route run. I expect Geno Smith to lean on his start receiver in Week 1 against a revamped Tennessee secondary. Alontae Taylor (2025: 68.9% catch rate and 107.5 passer rating) and Cor'Dale Flott (53% catch rate and 72.8 passer rating) aren't pushovers, but they also aren't elite and won't push Wilson out of my starting lineups for Week 1.

Emeka Egbuka faded after Week 5 last year after he sustained a hamstring injury, and Baker Mayfield's injury severely impacted his ability to feed catchable targets to the receiving options in Tampa Bay. In Weeks 1-5, Egbuka was the WR3 in fantasy points per game, commanding a 22.1% target share with 89 receiving yards per game, 2.71 yards per route run, a 26.1% first-read share, and 0.104 first downs per route run. Had Egbuka kept up that pace all season, he would have ranked 19th in target share, third in receiving yards per game, fourth in yards per route run, 26th in first-read share, and 20th in first downs per route run. Sadly, he didn't keep up that pace. In Weeks 6-18, despite still drawing a 23.1% target share with a 28.9% first-read share, Egbuka had only 41.1 receiving yards per game, 1.50 yards per route run, and 0.052 first downs per route run as the WR55 in fantasy points per game. Egbuka has dealt with a toe injury in camp, which is concerning, but his coverage and possible shadow matchups in Week 1 concern me more. Last year, Egbuka ran 63.5% of his routes from the perimeter, which means he could see D.J. Turner for most of Week 1. Last year, Turner was one of the best shutdown corners in the NFL, following D.K. Metcalf (twice), Justin Jefferson, Romeo Doubs, Zay Flowers (twice), and Gabe Davis on at least 60% of their routes. In those matchups, he allowed only one receiving touchdown, and only Jefferson surpassed 70 receiving yards in his coverage. An added worry is also Cincy's usage of single high (sixth-highest last year, 56.7%). Last year, when Egbuka was at the height of his powers (Weeks 1-5), against single high he only had 1.36 yards per route run. Egbuka could get by in Week 1 with volume and some timely slot usage to get him away from Turner, but I don't think it'll be a blow-up game.

injury.comment: Emeka Egbuka (toe) cleared for Week 1

news.title: Emeka Egbuka (toe) cleared for Week 1

fp.note: I'm not buying the offseason narratives that the Texans backfield will be a 50/50 split. David Montgomery will likely operate as the team's workhorse. Last year, he was phased out of the Lions' offensive plans as the season moved along, which led to his RB32 finish in fantasy points per game. In Weeks 12-18, he was the RB43 in fantasy points per game with a 32.1% snap rate, 8.2 touches per game, and only 42.8 total yards per game. Montgomery still has the juice to produce as a workhorse this season. Last season, he ranked 30th in missed tackle rate, but he was 12th in yards after contact per attempt. His receiving chops are also still alive and well, as he was also 22nd in yards per route run and 12th in first downs per route run. Last season, Montgomery bested Marks in explosive run rate, missed tackle rate, rushing success rate, yards after contact per attempt, and yards per route run. Legit, every per-touch metric that I care about. Montgomery is the superior back, even at this stage of his career. Montgomery should have a successful Week 1 against a run defense that last season (in Weeks 12-18) allowed the 13th-highest rushing success rate, the 14th-highest yards before contact per attempt, and had the 11th-lowest stuff rate.

It seems like George Kittle will be ready to rock for Week 1. Now, if he's active, will he play a full-time role for the 49ers? I doubt it, but he could still easily have a 50-60% snap rate and be heavily involved when they are passing and around the goal line. When Kittle was on the field last year, he didn't show any signs of slowing down. Among 54 qualifying tight ends, he ranked fourth in target share (20%) and yards per route run (2.30), third in receiving yards per game (57.1) and first-read share (24.3%), and second in first downs per route run (0.139). Kittle could have another amazing season in 2026 for fantasy, but I'm willing to sit him in Week 1 with the playing time concerns and a tough matchup. Last year, the Rams allowed the third-fewest yards per target and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Chuba Hubbard followed up his big breakout 2024 season with a stinker in 2025. Last year, Chuba Hubbard fell apart as the RB40 in fantasy points per game. Yes, he dealt with a calf injury for part of the season, but he also lost his starting job during the season to Rico Dowdle. Hubbard was arguably the most inefficient running back in the NFL last year. Among 49 qualifying backs, he ranked dead last in missed tackle rate and explosive run rate (zero explosive runs) while also sitting at 47th in yards after contact per attempt. I expect Jonathon Brooks to lead the backfield this season, but Hubbard should still be a sizable portion of the rushing attack to open the season. This gives him flex value with some upside for Week 1. The Bears' run defense struggled to close last season, and they didn't make any massive additions this offseason to give any hope that they'll be improved this year. Last season, in Weeks 12-18, Chicago allowed the highest rushing success rate, the sixth-most yards before contact per attempt, and the 11th-highest EPA per rush.

J.K. Dobbins should be Denver's early down hammer again this year. Last year, in Weeks 1-10, he was the RB24 in fantasy points per game, averaging 16.4 touches and 80.6 total yards. The bulk of that work was in the rushing department, as he averaged only 1.4 targets and 3.7 receiving yards per game. He had only four games in which he saw more than one target, and he never saw more than two targets in any game. Dobbins was on pace for 260 carries and 1,313 rushing yards before his injury, so his value on early downs is quite nice. Among 49 qualifying backs, he ranked third in explosive run rate and eighth in missed tackle rate. Dobbins should have a productive Week 1 against a run defense that last year allowed the eighth-highest zone rushing success rate (Dobbins 54.9% zone in 2025), had the tenth-lowest rate of hits at or behind the line of scrimmage, and ranked 17th in yards before contact per attempt.

Quentin Johnston could easily be the Bolts' WR1 this season because when he was healthy last season, that's exactly who he was. Last year, in Week 5, Johnston sustained a hamstring injury that lingered into his Week 7 and 8 usage (missed Week 6). In Weeks 7-8, Johnston had a 9.1% target share and zero targets (9.78% and zero first-read shares). Those were massive departures from his early-season usage and for the remainder of the season. In Weeks 1-4 and 9-18, when he was presumably healthy, Johnson had a 20.3% target share, 1.83 yards per route run, 12 red zone targets, 17 deep targets, a 27% missed tackle rate, and a 24.8% first-read share. During those games, Johnston led the team in EACH of those statistical categories while posting 13.9 PPR points per game. If Johnston had kept up that per-game output for fantasy all season, he would have been the WR16 in fantasy points per game. Johnston is a strong fantasy option for Week 1 against a secondary that allowed the ninth-most yards per target and ranked 16th in fantasy points per opportunity against perimeter wide receivers last year.

Deebo Samuel rejoins the San Francisco 49ers on a one-year deal after a one-year dalliance with the Commanders. Last year, Samuel was the WR29 in fantasy points per game while putting up a varied stat line. Last year, among 109 qualifying receivers, Samuel was 18th in target share (22.4%), ninth in yards after the catch per reception (6.6), 21st in first-read share (27.3%), and ninth-best in missed tackles forced per reception. Unfortunately, though, among the same sample of receivers, he was also 38th in yards per route run and 53rd in first downs per route run (0.076) while seeing his usual bevy of underneath targets (5.3 aDOT, 103rd out of 109 qualifying receivers). Last year, the Rams utilized zone coverage at the seventh-highest rate (76.4%). Over the last three seasons, against zone, Samuel has had a 23% target-per-route run rate and 2.06 yards per route run. Samuel is a viable PPR flex for Week 1, but the matchup is tough. Last year, the Rams allowed the 14th-fewest yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to receivers.

Denzel Boston was a baller in college. In his final season, he had the fifth-best contested catch rate (min ten contested targets) among FBS wide receivers while also posting 2.44 yards per route run. He finished college with a 79th percentile college dominator and an 86th percentile collegiate target share. The concern about Deshaun Watson's ability to feed him catchable targets is real. I'm not trotting Boston out in lineups in Week 1 because of that concern and the horrible matchup he's staring at. Last year, Jacksonville allowed the third-fewest yards per target and the eight-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

I'm concerned about Drake London's outlook for Week 1 with Cooper Rush under center. (Please, Jack Strand, save us.) Rush isn't the worst starting quarterback in the NFL for Week 1, but he isn't great, either. Last year, despite Michael Penix and Kirk Cousins, London was cooking last year before a PCL injury derailed his season in Week 11. In Weeks 1-10 last year, London was the WR6 in fantasy points per game. During that stretch, he was fourth in target share (30.3%), fourth in receiving yards per game (86.4), sixth in yards per route run (2.74), fifth in first-read share (37.6%), and seventh in first downs per route run (0.135). Rush isn't even on par with Penix or Cousins as a quarterback; thus lie the concerns for Week 1. The matchup for London also isn't great. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Pittsburgh allowed the 13th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity and ranked 16th in fantasy points per target versus perimeter wide receivers. Pittsburgh added Jamel Dean this offseason, so I'm expecting them to improve upon last season's stretch run numbers. The only hope for London is that he sees enough volume in Week 1 to outkick Rush's inefficiencies.

We'll have to see how much work Jeremiyah Love gets in Week 1, as he is still recovering from a preseason injury, but I expect him to still be heavily involved. Love practiced on a limited basis all week and has been listed as questionable. Across his last two years in college, he ranked inside the top 15 backs in each season in yards after contact per attempt, breakaway rate, and elusive rating (per PFF). He's also a stellar pass catcher, as evidenced by sitting at 17th in yards per route run among FBS backs last year and drawing a 10.9% target share. This offseason, the Bolts added Dalvin Tomlinson and Akheem Mesidor to the defensive front, but I don't know if that's enough for their run defense to take a huge leap forward. Last season, the Bolts allowed the eighth-highest explosive run rate, the 11th-highest rushing success rate, and the 13th-most yards before contact per attempt.

news.title: Jeremiyah Love (ankle) active for Week 1

fp.note: Last year was a disappointing season for Ladd McConkey. He finished as the WR34 in fantasy points per game, with eight weeks outside the top 36 wide receivers in weekly scoring. The hype was heavy in draft season for McConkey to post monster numbers in Mike McDaniel's offense. I love McConkey's talent, but found myself lower than the market and expectations for McConkey this season. Last year, among 109 qualifying receivers, he ranked 41st in separation and 15th in route win rate. Those aren't damning numbers at all. Last year, among the same subset of receivers, McConkey was 29th in target share (19.8%), 62nd in yards per route run (1.47), 37th in receiving yards per game (49.3), 46th in first-read share (20.4%), and 64th in first downs per route run. None of that screams "amazing WR2 for fantasy purposes with WR1 upside." Last year, Arizona was 16th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to wide receivers. McConkey should be in fantasy lineups in Week 1 with a middling matchup on deck.

news.title: Ladd McConkey (undisclosed) exits early Sunday

fp.note: D'Andre Swift arguably had a career year last season for the Bears as the RB16 in fantasy points per game. He finished with 257 touches and 1,386 total yards while splitting work with Kyle Monangai. Monangai's presence didn't hurt Swift a ton, as he was the RB20 in fantasy points per game after Monangai's emergence in Week 9. During Weeks 10-18, Swift remained the preferred passing down back for Chicago with a 43% route share (Monangai 28.8%), but he split up the red zone work with Monangai, with 18 red zone rushing attempts to Monangai's 19. Last year, Swift's per-touch efficiency bounced back as he ranked 13th in explosive run rate, 11th in rushing success rate, and 20th in missed tackle rate. Swift should have a nice Week 1. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Carolina allowed the 13th-most yards before contact per attempt, the ninth-highest missed tackle rate, and the seventh-most EPA per rush.

Last year, Kyle Pitts had a tale of two seasons. Yes, overall it was a wonderful year as the TE5 in fantasy points per game and easily his best statistical season since his rookie year, but it was wildly different with Drake London in and out of the lineup. Without London, Pitts had a 26.7% target share with 84.4 receiving yards per game, 2.81 yards per route run, a 27.8% first-read share, 0.120 first downs per route run, and 19 fantasy points per game. Those are all elite numbers, and if Pitts had put up those stats all year, especially the fantasy points per game, he would have been the TE1 for fantasy. The problem is that with Drake London active, Pitts had a 19% target share, 42.2 receiving yards per game, 1.43 yards per route run, a 20.2% first-read share, 0.093 first downs per route run, and 9.6 fantasy points per game. All of those per-route metrics were still quite strong, but the fantasy points per game mark would have made Pitts the TE20 last year. London will be on the field for Week 1, and now Kyle Pitts has to deal with the quarterbacking rollercoaster of Cooper Rush. The small ray of hope for Pitts in Week 1 is that Pittsburgh struggled to defend tight ends to close last season, but they added Jaquan Brisker to the secondary this offseason. Maybe Brisker can help improve their defense against tight ends, but at the moment that's just a hopeful projection. Pitts will have to overcome London's target-hogging presence and Cooper Rush in Week 1 to post a solid stat line. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Pittsburgh allowed the 12th-most yards per target and the sixth-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Last year, after taking over as the Giants' starter, Jaxson Dart was the QB7 in fantasy points per game. If you remove the wet fart game that he had in Week 16 against Minnesota, where he scored only one fantasy point and had 13 pass attempts and 33 passing yards, he averaged 22.5 fantasy points per game. That points-per-game mark would have made him the QB1 in fantasy points per game last year. Dart showed off his rushing ability, averaging seven rushing attempts and 40.6 rushing yards per game. He had the second-most rushing yards per game among quarterbacks last year, behind only Justin Fields. Dart also wasn't a lackluster passer last year. Among 38 qualifying passers, he was 23rd in CPOE, 19th in highly accurate throw rate, and tenth in hero throw rate. Dart was also fifth in fantasy points per dropback while dealing with the 12th-highest drop rate among quarterbacks. The Giants' second-year signal-caller will face a revamped Dallas pass defense that added Rashan Gary, Cobie Durant, Jalen Thompson, and Caleb Downs this offseason. They'll be a much improved unit for 2026, but the question is how much? Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Dallas's pass defense was almost non-existent as they allowed the most fantasy points per dropback, the second-most yards per attempt, and the fifth-highest CPOE. Dallas should be viewed at least as a league-average matchup for Dart, with the upside to be a very good one.

Over the last two years, Travis Kelce has been the TE9 and TE7 in fantasy points per game. Travis Kelce's per-route efficiency screams that he's on the back nine of his career. Last year, among 59 qualifying tight ends, Kelce was 19th in yards per route run, 18th in yards after the catch per reception, and 16th in first downs per route run. Last year, Denver was 19th in yards per target versus tight ends while allowing the fourth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to the position. Kelce should see solid volume in Week 1. I don't think he'll have a monster game, but if he can get into the endzone he could possibly salvage a low-end TE1 outing.

Last year, Chris Godwin had a slow ramp-up in 2025, coming off a horrific ankle fracture in 2024. After coming back in Week 5, he had a fibula injury that delayed his return to a full-time role until Week 13. Once he was back, in Weeks 13-18 (59.7% slot), he had a 16.8% target share, 49.8 receiving yards per game, 1.88 yards per route run, a 21.2% first-read share, and 0.107 first downs per route run. The yards per route run and first downs per route run in that stretch loudly state that Chris Godwin isn't washed or over the hill, as he was also the WR32 in fantasy points per game. Baker Mayfield could lean heavily on Godwin if Emeka Egbuka is being followed by DJ Turner all day. The coverage matchup for Godwin could also work in his favor. Last year, Cincy utilized single high at the sixth-highest rate (56.7%). In Weeks 13-18, Godwin had 1.71 yards per route run and a 21.3% first-read share against single high. Cincy was also horrible at defending the slot, giving up the fifth-most yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Kenneth Gainwell was an integral part of the Pittsburgh backfield last year for the entire season, but he really hit his stride in Weeks 11-18 as the RB7 in fantasy points per game with 13.3 touches and 85 total yards per game. His passing game usage was robust during this stretch as he was third in target share (17.5%), second in receiving yards per game (45.4), fourth in yards per route run (2.10), and first in first downs per route run (0.116). That also isn't to say that he wasn't also fantastic on early downs, ranking 14th in explosive run rate and missed tackle rate overall for the season among backs. All of the reports out of camp are that Gainwell will split the work with Bucky Irving this season, much like Rachaad White has in previous seasons. It's tough projecting this matchup with all of the moves the Cincy made this offseason to overhaul their defensive line with the additions of Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, Boye Mafe, and Cashius Howell. I'm treating it as a neutral matchup with the ability to be a positive one for Gainwell on the ground. Last year, Cincy allowed the seventh-highest explosive run rate and rushing success rate and the fourth-most yards before contact per attempt to backs. Even if Cincy is improved as a defense against the run, they didn't massively overhaul their linebacker room, so Gainwell could eat through the air. Last year, Cincy allowed the sixth-most yards per target, the second-most YAC/reception, and the third-most yards per route run to backs.

At this point in his career, we know who Khalil Shakir is. A low-ceiling WR3/4 or flex play on a weekly basis in PPR formats. Over the last two seasons, he has finished as the WR39 and WR33 in fantasy points per game. Last year, among 109 qualifying receivers, Shakir was 36th in target share, 55th in receiving yards per game, 41st in yards per route run, 38th in first-read share, and 80th in first downs per route run. This isn't the week to consider flexing Shakir. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Houston allowed the 11th-fewest fantasy points per game to receiving yards and the tenth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers.

Last year, Bo Nix regressed as a passer, and with his overall production, he was still the QB11 in fantasy points per game. Nix saw his passing touchdown rate fall from 5.1% to 4.1%, and his rushing yards per game dip from 25.3 to 20.9 (16th). Nix still directed a passing offense that was fifth in neutral passing rate and tenth in neutral pace. I don't see either of those figures changing in 2026. If anything, Denver could easily be top five in neutral pace this season with all of the news coming out of the Broncos' camp this offseason about new playcaller Davis Webb. Among 38 qualifying passers, he was 31st in yards per attempt, 18th in highly accurate throw rate, 19th in hero throw rate, and 22nd in fantasy points per dropback. Last year, in his two regular season meetings with Kansas City, Nix was the QB19 and QB10 in weekly fantasy scoring. He could easily be a QB1 this week against a pass defense that allowed the 13th-highest passer rating last year while ranking 19th in passing success rate and 18th in EPA per dropback allowed.

Jordan Mason is a one-trick pony, but that one trick is quite good. He's a strong early-down option for NFL offenses and should continue to serve in the role this season for Minnesota. Last year, he was the RB42 in fantasy points per game while soaking up 158 rushing attempts and producing 758 rushing yards and six total touchdowns. Among 49 qualifying backs, he ranked tenth in explosive run rate, seventh in rushing success rate, ninth in missed tackle rate, and 15th in yards after contact per attempt. Aaron Jones will continue to be the passing-down partner for Mason for Minny in 2026. Mason is a viable touchdown-dependent flex for Week 1. Last year, Green Bay allowed the sixth-lowest explosive run rate and the fifth-fewest yards after contact per attempt while ranking 15th in yards before contact per attempt and rushing success rate allowed.

Bucky Irving has dealt with a number of injuries in his short career with a foot sprain and a shoulder/ AC joint sprain last year. Rewinding to 2024, he also dealt with hip, back, toe, and hamstring issues. When he was on the field last year, he averaged 20.3 touches and 86.5 total yards as the RB17 in fantasy points per game. His efficiency suffered massively from the injuries last year after being a wondrous per-touch monster in 2024. Last year, among 49 qualifying backs, he was 43rd in explosive run rate, 35th in missed tackle rate, and 46th in yards after contact per attempt. Those dips are explainable, but they are still concerning for a back that is on the smaller side and has been banged up quite often over the last two seasons. Yes, Rachaad White is gone, but Irving will still have to contend with Kenneth Gainwell in what I'm projecting to be a split backfield. It's tough projecting this matchup with all of the moves the Cincy made this offseason to overhaul their defensive line with the additions of Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, Boye Mafe, and Cashius Howell. I'm treating it as a neutral matchup with the ability to be a positive one for Irving. Last year, Cincy allowed the seventh-highest explosive run rate and rushing success rate and the fourth-most yards before contact per attempt to backs.

Marvin Harrison Jr. had a troubled 2025 season as he dealt with a concussion, an appendectomy, and a heel injury that cost him five games. In the eight games he played last year before dealing with appendicitis and a heel injury, he garnered a 21.9% target share, producing 61.6 receiving yards per game with 1.68 yards per route run, a 27.1% first-read share, and 0.082 first downs per route run. During that stretch, he averaged 13.4 PPR points per game. It's a BIG if, but if he had kept up that type of production, he would have been the WR17 in fantasy points per game. Last year, if you put up that sample for Harrison Jr. against all wide receivers with at least 200 routes, he would have ranked 19th in target share, 16th in receiving yards per game, 44th in yards per route run, 23rd in first-read share, and 46th in first downs per route run. We'll see if Harrison Jr. can pick up where he left off in Week 1 against a secondary that last year allowed the 11th-fewest receiving yards per game and the fifth-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Rico Dowdle did it again last season. Dowdle fought to get to the top of the Carolina running back depth chart as he wrestled the starting job away from Chuba Hubbard. In Weeks 5-18, Dowdle averaged 18.6 touches and 87.7 total yards as the RB10 in fantasy points per game. Dowdle also excelled last season on the ground and in the receiving game. He ranked 23rd in explosive run rate, 17th in missed tackle rate, tenth in yards after contact per attempt, 17th in yards per route run, and 16th in first downs per route run. After that strong season, Dowdle now finds himself reunited with Mike McCarthy in Pittsburgh as a backfield complement to Jaylen Warren. Dowdle can't be counted on for more than a flex play for Week 1, with his usage up in the air. If Dowdle does get into the end zone in Week 1, he could easily pay off as a flex, though. Atlanta was a middle-of-the-road run defense last year to close the season. In Weeks 12-18, Atlanta was 15th in stuff rate and rushing success rate allowed while also ranking 16th in yards before contact per attempt.

Last year was the second time in Dallas Goedert's career that he finished as a top-six fantasy tight end (TE6 in fantasy points per game). Goedert accomplished this by spiking a career-high 11 receiving touchdowns. Last year, among 59 qualifying tight ends, Goedert ranked eighth in target share (18.4%), 33rd in yards per route run (1.43), 17th in receiving yards per game (39.4), eighth in first-read share (21%), seventh in red zone targets (15), and 21st in first downs per route run (0.083). Washington added a lot of firepower to their pass rush and secondary this offseason, but we'll see how much and how quickly they can improve a defense that allowed the most yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends last year.

Blake Corum is a viable touchdown-dependent flex this week with a good matchup. Last year, in Weeks 7-18, Corum helped Kyren Williams with the heavy lifting on early downs, averaging 10.5 rushing attempts and 53.6 rushing yards. He didn't offer much through the air during that stretch with only seven targets and 27 receiving yards. If you're looking to flex Corum this week, he'll have to pay off in the rushing department and (hopefully) fall into the end zone. Last year, among 49 qualifying backs, Corum ranked sixth in explosive run rate and 11th in missed tackle rate. Last year, San Francisco allowed the highest rushing success rate, the tenth-most yards before contact per attempt, and had the seventh-lowest hit rate at or behind the line of scrimmage.

Mark Andrews is coming off his worst season in the NFL as the TE23 in fantasy points per game. Last year, Baltimore limited his playing time, as he was 22nd in route share (62.9%, per Fantasy Points Data). I'm expecting that to rebound in 2026 with Isaiah Likely gone, but we still have to see it materialize. Last year, among 59 qualifying tight ends, Andrews was ninth in first-read share, but his yards per route run (41st) and first downs per route run (27th) were nothing to write home about. Andrews could have a nice game in Week 1 that quells some of my concerns about his 2026 season. Last year, Indy allowed the fourth-most yards per target and the 12th-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends. Lou Anarumo's defenses have bled out production to tight ends over the years, so this wasn't a one-year isolated incident. I think it transfers over to 2026.

Patrick Mahomes saw his season end in Week 15 last year with a torn ACL. Prior to that horrible injury, he was the QB2 in fantasy points per game. Last year, he averaged a career-high 6.6 rushing attempts per game and 30.1 rushing yards per game. He was first in scrambles per game and 14th in red zone carries per game among quarterbacks. I don't expect those numbers to repeat this season coming off the ACL injury. Mahomes will work from the pocket more in 2026, especially to open the season. Last year, outside of the immense passing volume he saw, it was an uninspiring year for Mahomes as an accurate passer. Among 38 qualifying passers, he was 18th in yards per attempt, 24th in adjusted completion rate, 16th in highly accurate throw rate, and 30th in catchable target rate. Denver is a tough test out of the gate for Mahomes. Last year, Denver allowed the second-fewest yards per attempt, the sixth-lowest passer rating, the second-lowest passing success rate, and the sixth-fewest EPA per dropback.

Rashee Rice had another "interesting offseason" where he had a knee scope and spent some time rehabbing from that procedure in a jail cell. Rice hasn't played more than eight games in a season since 2023, so while he has been very productive when he's been on the field over the last two seasons, we still haven't seen him available for a full calendar of football since that season. Last year, when he was on the field, Rice remained a target hog with a 26.2% target share (12th among 109 qualifying receivers), averaging 71.4 receiving yards per game (tenth), producing 2.28 yards per route run (15th), and churning out 0.112 first downs per route run with a 31.9% first-read share (both 14th-best). Rice could see a heavy workload in Week 1, but I don't know that he'll have a ton of productivity with it against a secondary that allowed the second-fewest yards per target and the fewest fantasy points per opportunity to wide receivers last season.

Last year, Tetairoa McMillan had a strong rookie season as the WR20 in fantasy points per game despite a limited passing-volume offense and up-and-down quarterback play from Bryce Young. Last year, in Weeks 3-18, Young surpassed 35 passing attempts only once, had only two games with more than 225 passing yards, and directed an offense that was fifth in neutral rushing rate. Last year, McMillan, among 109 qualifying receivers, ranked 14th in target share (23.1%), 19th in receiving yards per game (59.6), 27th in yards per route run (1.94), 15th in first-read share (28.5%), and 17th in first downs per route run (0.105). Last year, to close the season in Weeks 17-20, Chicago leaned into single high coverage as a pass defense (58.2%). McMillan was excellent against single-high last year with a 26% target-per-route run rate and 2.06 yards per route run. McMillan could easily begin the season with a standout Week 1. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Chicago allowed the second-most yards per target and the fifth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Jameson Williams had a tale-of-two-halves season in 2025. There are a lot of reasons why it worked out that way that I'll dive into shortly. In Weeks 1-9, he was the WR46 in fantasy points per game with a 14.9% target share (15.2 aDOT), 44.4 receiving yards per game, 1.54 yards per route run, a 14.9% first-read share, and 0.074 first downs per route run. During this stretch, Williams was just the low-volume field-stretching option while Sam LaPorta was healthy. John Morton was still calling plays, and it looked like Williams was on his way to a bust season. Then Sam LaPorta was lost for the season in Week 10, and Dan Campbell took over play-calling duties, and everything changed for the Detroit speedster. In Weeks 10-18, Williams was the WR11 in fantasy points per game while seeing an 18.5% target share (11.5 aDOT) with 84.7 receiving yards per game, 2.34 yards per route run, a 21.1% first-read share, and 0.098 first downs per route run. Williams' target share and first-read share put him in the WR2/3 bucket, while his per-route efficiency and three 100-yard receiving games vaulted him higher. His aDOT came down, and he was more involved weekly as a central cog of the offense. So the question is which version of Williams will we see in 2026? Well, that's tough to say because Drew Petzing will be calling plays, and he has had his own struggles in previous seasons putting wide receivers in the best spot to produce (hello, Marvin Harrison Jr.). If this game against the Saints turns into a shootout, Williams could have a strong Week 1, but I wouldn't trust him as more than a WR3/flex to open the season. The Saints secondary was stout to close last season. In Weeks 12-18, they allowed the second-lowest yards per target and the fifth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Jadarian Price was selected in the first round of the NFL Draft by the Seahawks to be their new Kenneth Walker (and maybe more). Walker led the backfield last year for Seattle, but they limited his usage in the red zone and in the passing game. Price remains an unknown in the passing game after only 13 targets over the last two collegiate seasons at Notre Dame. Price is a wonderful rushing talent ranking 25th and fifth in yards after contact per attempt, 31st and 3rd in breakaway rate, and 15th and 39th in elusive rating over the last two seasons in college (per PFF). Price could find plenty of running room in Week 1 with a Seattle rushing attack that was seventh in zone rushing rate last year. Last season, New England held backs to the fifth-lowest explosive run rate, but they also gave up the ninth-highest rushing success rate, had the 11th-lowest stuff rate, and surrendered the fourth-highest zone rushing success rate.

Harold Fannin Jr. had a banner rookie season as the TE8 in fantasy points per game. Last year, among 54 qualifying tight ends, Fannin was fifth in target share (19.4%), 12th in receiving yards per game (45.7), 12th in yards per route run (1.81), fourth in first-read share (22.3%), and 25th in first downs per route run. I expect Fannin Jr.'s numbers to dip some with more target competition around him this season. I don't expect him to begin 2026 with a bang in Week 1, either. Last year, Jacksonville allowed the sixth-fewest yards per target and the eight-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Jonathon Brooks is a nice flex with upside in Week 1. He should at least split the work with Chuba Hubbard to open the season, with the upside to be the clear lead runner from the jump. Just to remind everyone about the talent that Brooks has, in 2024 (his final collegiate season), he ranked 21st in yards after contact per attempt, ninth in elusive rating, and 21st in yards per route run (per PFF). The Bears' run defense struggled to close last season, and they didn't make any massive additions this offseason to give any hope that they'll be improved this year. Last season, in Weeks 12-18, Chicago allowed the highest rushing success rate, the sixth-most yards before contact per attempt, and the 11th-highest EPA per rush.

news.title: Jonathon Brooks (groin) not expected to face snap count Sunday

fp.note: Brian Thomas Jr. was one of the biggest busts of the 2025 season. He dealt with a high ankle sprain and a shoulder issue and never looked like the player we all loved during his rookie season. Once Thomas Jr. was "healthy" and Jakobi Meyers was on the roster, Thomas was relegated to a field-stretching role. In Weeks 13-18, he had only two top-24 outings in weekly scoring (WR15, WR23) with a 14.9% target share (18.1 aDOT), 47.8 receiving yards per game, 1.65 yards per route run, three red zone targets, and a 20.6% first-read share. If Thomas Jr. is going to have a bounce-back campaign, I don't think it starts in Week 1. Last year, when Tyson Campbell and Denzel Ward were on the field together as full-time players, the Cleveland pass defense was a shutdown unit against perimeter wide receivers. In their eight games together, the Browns' pass defense allowed only 1.43 fantasy points per target and 7.24 yards per target to perimeter wide receivers. Over the entire season, those would have been the third-lowest marks in each category in the NFL. In that sample, Cleveland was also elite at defending against deep passing, giving up only a 31% completion rate and a 73.1 passer rating. Over the entire season, those would have ranked as sixth-best and seventh-best against deep passing.

injury.comment: Thomas Jr. suffered the apparent shoulder injury in the second quarter of the Week 1 contest, hauling in all three of his targets for 40 yards prior to exiting.

news.title: Brian Thomas Jr. (shoulder) questionable to return

fp.note: Josh Downs dealt with a hamstring issue to open last season, which could be a reason why he didn't eclipse a 60% snap share until Week 4. Downs' playing time was a rollercoaster the rest of the season, as his snap rate dipped below 60% in five other weeks in the remainder of the season. Originally, Downs was expected to step into an elevated role in 2026 and play more on the perimeter after seeing only 65 routes as a boundary receiver last year. I worry that plan could be scrapped after the signing of Keenan Allen. Downs could easily be in his limited snap slot role again in 2026. Maybe not out of the gate with Alec Pierce getting back up to full speed, but it's still up in the air. Last year, overall, Downs was 19th in separation score and 55th in route win rate, but when you look at him as a perimeter receiver, he drops to 52nd in separation and 84th in route win rate. On a per-route basis, among 109 qualifying receivers, he was 29th in target per route run rate, 66th in yards per route run, and 26th in first downs per route run. I'm not plugging Downs into a lineup in Week 1 with his playing time up in the air. The matchup also isn't a smash one to worry about missing out on. The Ravens should field an improved pass defense this season, but last year their secondary wasn't hopeless against receivers. They allowed the 11th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity and ranked 15th in yards per target.

R.J. Harvey's rookie season was a tale of two seasons centered around J.K. Dobbins being in the lineup and out of it. In Weeks 1-10, Harvey was the RB29 in fantasy points per game, averaging 29.1% of the snaps played with 7.5 touches and 38.9 total yards per game. In Weeks 11-18, with Dobbins out, he was the RB13 in fantasy points per game with 16.8 touches and 72.5 total yards per game while averaging 60.7% of the snaps played. With Dobbins back, I'm expecting Harvey to be the primary passing down back for Denver. As a pass catcher, he ranked sixth in target per route run rate and first downs per route run and tenth in yards per route run. Harvey is a PPR-focused flex play for Week 1. Last year, Kansas City allowed the 13th-most yards per target to running backs while ranking 17th in fantasy points per game allowed to receiving production.
