In Weeks 6-18, despite still drawing a 23.1% target share with a 28.9% first-read share, Egbuka had only 41.1 receiving yards per game, 1.50 yards per route run, and 0.052 first downs per route run as the WR55 in fantasy points per game. Egbuka has dealt with a toe injury in camp, which is concerning, but his coverage and possible shadow matchups in Week 1 concern me more. Last year, Egbuka ran 63.5% of his routes from the perimeter, which means he could see D.J. Turner for most of Week 1. Last year, Turner was one of the best shutdown corners in the NFL, following D.K. Metcalf (twice), Justin Jefferson, Romeo Doubs, Zay Flowers (twice), and Gabe Davis on at least 60% of their routes. In those matchups, he allowed only one receiving touchdown, and only Jefferson surpassed 70 receiving yards in his coverage. An added worry is also Cincy's usage of single high (sixth-highest last year, 56.7%). Last year, when Egbuka was at the height of his powers (Weeks 1-5), against single high he only had 1.36 yards per route run. Egbuka could get by in Week 1 with volume and some timely slot usage to get him away from Turner, but I don't think it'll be a blow-up game.

injury.comment: Emeka Egbuka (toe) cleared for Week 1

news.title: Emeka Egbuka (toe) cleared for Week 1

fp.note: Before his 2025 season was lost to a back injury, Sam LaPorta was the TE7 in fantasy points per game. The back has healed up well over the offseason. Despite the injury-shortened season, LaPorta was still one of the most explosive tight ends in the NFL on a per-route basis. Among 59 qualifying tight ends, he ranked tenth in target share (17.8%), sixth in receiving yards per game (54.3), fifth in yards per route run (2.14), and eighth in first downs per route run (0.100). LaPorta doesn't have the best matchup to open the season, but he could still get in the end zone and finish as a TE1 in Week 1. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, New Orleans allowed the ninth-fewest yards per target and the third-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Stefon Diggs will be Terry McLaurin's running mate this season. Diggs had a strong 2025 season that proved that he has plenty left in the tank to post a strong fantasy season in 2026. Last year, he was the WR23 in fantasy points per game with only a 65.4% route share (62nd out of 109 qualifying receivers). Among 109 qualifying receivers, he was stellar on a per-route basis, ranking 22nd in target per route run rate (25%), 20th in receiving yards per game (59.6), and eighth in yards per route run (2.53) and first downs per route run (0.127). Among the same sample of receivers, he was also 28th in overall separation score, 18th in separation versus man coverage, 22nd in route win rate against man coverage, and 11th in yards per route run against both man and zone coverages. Last year in Washington's two meetings with Philly, the Eagles utilized two-high with 60.4% of their defensive snaps. Last year, against two high, Diggs had a 26% target per route run rate and 2.24 yards per route run. Those are both stellar numbers, and with the consolidated target tree in Washington, I expect Diggs to see healthy volume in Week 1. I just worry about his ceiling with this tough matchup. Last year, Philly allowed the third-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Last year, Chris Godwin had a slow ramp-up in 2025, coming off a horrific ankle fracture in 2024. After coming back in Week 5, he had a fibula injury that delayed his return to a full-time role until Week 13. Once he was back, in Weeks 13-18 (59.7% slot), he had a 16.8% target share, 49.8 receiving yards per game, 1.88 yards per route run, a 21.2% first-read share, and 0.107 first downs per route run. The yards per route run and first downs per route run in that stretch loudly state that Chris Godwin isn't washed or over the hill, as he was also the WR32 in fantasy points per game. Baker Mayfield could lean heavily on Godwin if Emeka Egbuka is being followed by DJ Turner all day. The coverage matchup for Godwin could also work in his favor. Last year, Cincy utilized single high at the sixth-highest rate (56.7%). In Weeks 13-18, Godwin had 1.71 yards per route run and a 21.3% first-read share against single high. Cincy was also horrible at defending the slot, giving up the fifth-most yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Jonathon Brooks is a nice flex with upside in Week 1. He should at least split the work with Chuba Hubbard to open the season, with the upside to be the clear lead runner from the jump. Just to remind everyone about the talent that Brooks has, in 2024 (his final collegiate season), he ranked 21st in yards after contact per attempt, ninth in elusive rating, and 21st in yards per route run (per PFF). The Bears' run defense struggled to close last season, and they didn't make any massive additions this offseason to give any hope that they'll be improved this year. Last season, in Weeks 12-18, Chicago allowed the highest rushing success rate, the sixth-most yards before contact per attempt, and the 11th-highest EPA per rush.

news.title: Jonathon Brooks (groin) not expected to face snap count Sunday

fp.note: Jordan Love has been a mid-range QB2 over the last two years (QB17, QB16) since his massive breakout in 2023 (QB5), but that hasn't been because Love sucks. He has been locked in a run-first, run-always offense. Could that still be the case this year? Possibly, but if Green Bay increases its pass rate to even league-average standards (last year, Weeks 1-15, eighth-best in neutral rushing rate), Love could return to QB1 land. The last time that we saw this Green Bay offense without Josh Jacobs was 2023, when Love was dealing. Maybe Matt LaFleur lets Jordan Love cook until we get clarity about Jacobs' 2026 outlook. Love has proven over the last three seasons that he can sustain above-average passing touchdown rates (5.5%, 5.9%, 5.2%), so I don't see him backsliding in that category. Last year, among 38 qualifying quarterbacks, Love was eighth in yards per attempt, fifth in hero throw rate, 15th in catchable target rate, and 13th (tied) in fantasy points per dropback. Love will have his hands full to open the 2026 season with Brian Flores' defense that in Weeks 12-18 last year allowed the seventh-fewest yards per attempt, the third-lowest passer rating, and ranked 17th in passing success rate. Love could succeed, though, because of his ability to stand tall against the blitz. Over the last two years, Minnesota has led the league each season in blitz rate. Over the last two seasons, among 37 qualifying passers, Love has ranked seventh in yards per attempt and EPA per dropback and 17th in passing success rate against the blitz. I'm betting on Love to have a strong showing in Week 1.

I have no clue what to expect for Terrance Ferguson's Week 1 usage for the Rams. Last year, Ferguson had only a 34.2% route share, a 5.5% target share, a 15% target-per-route run rate, and a 7.6% first-read share. The reports out of camp and during this offseason were that he should see an expanded role in year two, but the Rams can be truthful in that estimation without having a high bar to clear. Last year, among 54 qualifying tight ends, he was 48th in target-per-route-run rate and 32nd in yards per route run. He was essentially their deep threat with a wild 18.3 aDOT. I would have to be desperate in a DEEP league to start Ferguson for Week 1. Last year, the 49ers allowed the fifth-fewest yards per target to tight ends, but they also surrendered the sixth-most receiving touchdowns to the position. Ferguson is likely a touchdown-or-bust dart throw for Week 1.

D.J. Moore's stock took a tumble last year as Moore sank to WR41 in fantasy points per game. Moore had a 14.3% target share with 1.33 yards per route run, a 17.5% first-read share, and 0.063 first downs per route run. None of these numbers offer hope for 2026, but don't tune out just yet. Last year, among 109 qualifying receivers, Moore was 47th and 49th in separation score and route win rate. The numbers get even better when we look at Moore as a perimeter receiver, which he'll be asked to do more than the 65% of snaps that he played there last year. As an outside receiver last year, among the same sample of receivers, he was 36th in separation and 29th in route win rate. Moore has a tough matchup out of the gate against the Houston Texans. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, against perimeter wide receivers, they allowed the 11th-fewest fantasy points per game to receiving yards and the 14th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity. Moore should get peppered with volume, which should help him in this difficult matchup, but I'm not projecting a monster performance from him in Week 1.

Jadarian Price was selected in the first round of the NFL Draft by the Seahawks to be their new Kenneth Walker (and maybe more). Walker led the backfield last year for Seattle, but they limited his usage in the red zone and in the passing game. Price remains an unknown in the passing game after only 13 targets over the last two collegiate seasons at Notre Dame. Price is a wonderful rushing talent ranking 25th and fifth in yards after contact per attempt, 31st and 3rd in breakaway rate, and 15th and 39th in elusive rating over the last two seasons in college (per PFF). Price could find plenty of running room in Week 1 with a Seattle rushing attack that was seventh in zone rushing rate last year. Last season, New England held backs to the fifth-lowest explosive run rate, but they also gave up the ninth-highest rushing success rate, had the 11th-lowest stuff rate, and surrendered the fourth-highest zone rushing success rate.

Michael Wilson had Grand Canyon-sized splits last year when Marvin Harrison Jr. was out of the lineup versus when he was healthy. In the eight games Harrison Jr. was active before his heel injury and was healthy, Wilson had only an 11.7% target share, 23.4 receiving yards per game, 0.72 yards per route run, and a 14.1% first-read share. That isn't remotely close to fantasy-viable production. In the games Harrison Jr. missed and during Weeks 16 & 17 (after Harrison Jr returned post heel injury), Wilson was absolutely fantastic with a 27.5% target share, 105.6 receiving yards per game, 2.79 yards per route run, and a 38.8% first-read share (23.3 PPR points per game). That is elite WR1-level production and efficiency. Unfortunately for Wilson, Harrison Jr. is healthy to begin the season, and they are both staring at a touch matchup for Week 1 against a secondary that last year allowed the 11th-fewest receiving yards per game and the fifth-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers. Sit Wilson for Week 1.

R.J. Harvey's rookie season was a tale of two seasons centered around J.K. Dobbins being in the lineup and out of it. In Weeks 1-10, Harvey was the RB29 in fantasy points per game, averaging 29.1% of the snaps played with 7.5 touches and 38.9 total yards per game. In Weeks 11-18, with Dobbins out, he was the RB13 in fantasy points per game with 16.8 touches and 72.5 total yards per game while averaging 60.7% of the snaps played. With Dobbins back, I'm expecting Harvey to be the primary passing down back for Denver. As a pass catcher, he ranked sixth in target per route run rate and first downs per route run and tenth in yards per route run. Harvey is a PPR-focused flex play for Week 1. Last year, Kansas City allowed the 13th-most yards per target to running backs while ranking 17th in fantasy points per game allowed to receiving production.

Last year, we only got to see Kyler Murray for five games. In the previous six seasons, he had never finished lower than QB12 in fantasy points per game. Last year, in his limited starting sample before being sidelined with a foot injury, Murray had the seventh-lowest yards per attempt, the fourth-lowest aDOT, and the fifth-lowest hero throw rate. None of those numbers will make you feel warm and fuzzy, but maybe Kevin O'Connell can sprinkle some of his Minnesota magic glitter on Murray and his level of quarterbacking improves in 2026. We shall see. I'm not hopeful that Murray begins the 2026 season with a monster game, though. Last year, Green Bay allowed the sixth-fewest yards per attempt, the 14th-lowest passing success rate, and the ninth-fewest fantasy points per dropback to quarterbacks. Also, looking at Jonathon Gannon's coverage structure gives me worries for Murray without even stating that Gannon has innate knowledge of what Murray excels at and what he struggles with. Since 2023, Gannon has utilized two high at the third-highest rate (57.6%). Over the last two seasons, among 31 qualifying passers, against two high, Murray has had the 14th-lowest yards per attempt, the 13th-lowest highly accurate throw rate, and the ninth-fewest fantasy points per dropback against two high.

injury.comment: Murray suffered the apparent concussion in the first quarter after being hit by Green Bay safety Jevon Bullard, with backup Carson Wentz taking over behind center for head coach Kevin O’Connell.

news.title: Kyler Murray (concussion) ruled out Sunday

fp.note: Hunter is expected to log the majority of his snaps at corner in Week 1, but should still see at least a handful of plays on the offensive side of the ball. As a corner alone, he is an INT-heavy league option only, but with the extra few points he can get from a reception or two against Cleveland, makes him worth a long look as a DB2 option. The Browns offense is in flux, and Deshaun Watson is going to be ripe for a pick or two in his first NFL game action in over 700 days. Start Hunter where needed.

With Brock Bowers out for a few games and sidelined for Week 1, Michael Mayer will step into a bigger role. Last year, he was utilized sparingly with a 44.4% route share, but when he was on the field, he was productive. Last season, among 54 qualifying tight ends, Mayer was tenth in target per route run rate (23%), 23rd in yards per route run (1.57), and 19th in first downs per route run (0.086). Mayer could easily flirt with TE1 production in Week 1 against a defense that last season allowed the ninth-most yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

I'm expecting Cam Skattebo to retain his lead back role to open the 2026 season, but we'll have to see if that is a bellcow role or just the leader of a committee backfield. The human battering ram known as Cam Skattebo made waves in his rookie season before being sidelined by a horrible ankle/fibula fracture that also ruptured his deltoid ligament in Week 8 of last season. In Weeks 2-7 as the Giants' workhorse, Skattebo averaged 19.5 touches and 96.3 total yards as the RB8 in fantasy points per game. Last season, he was stellar with his touches, ranking fourth in missed tackle rate and yards after contact per attempt, 11th in target per route run rate, eighth in yards per route run, and second in first downs per route run. Skattebo will face an uphill climb in Week 1 against a Dallas run defense that found its footing after the acquisition of Quinnen Williams last season. In Weeks 11-18 last year, Dallas allowed the fifth-lowest rushing success rate, the seventh-fewest yards after contact per attempt, and had the fourth-best stuff rate.

D'Andre Swift arguably had a career year last season for the Bears as the RB16 in fantasy points per game. He finished with 257 touches and 1,386 total yards while splitting work with Kyle Monangai. Monangai's presence didn't hurt Swift a ton, as he was the RB20 in fantasy points per game after Monangai's emergence in Week 9. During Weeks 10-18, Swift remained the preferred passing down back for Chicago with a 43% route share (Monangai 28.8%), but he split up the red zone work with Monangai, with 18 red zone rushing attempts to Monangai's 19. Last year, Swift's per-touch efficiency bounced back as he ranked 13th in explosive run rate, 11th in rushing success rate, and 20th in missed tackle rate. Swift should have a nice Week 1. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Carolina allowed the 13th-most yards before contact per attempt, the ninth-highest missed tackle rate, and the seventh-most EPA per rush.

Over the last two seasons, Courtland Sutton has been the unquestioned WR1 for Bo Nix and the Denver Broncos. In those seasons, he finished as the WR18 and WR24 in fantasy points per game. The arrival of Jaylen Waddle will change that this year. Sutton still can be a highly productive player in a pass-happy offense, but he'll take a backseat to Waddle. Sutton's per-route data remained solid, but it wasn't spectacular outside of his separation score and route win rate (20th, ninth). Last year, among 109 qualifying receivers, Sutton was 35th in target per route run rate, 32nd in yards per route run, and 29th in first downs per route run. We'll see how quickly the new (or throwback, depending on how you choose to view it) look Kansas City corner room can hit the ground running with Nohl Williams (2025: 52.6% catch rate and 85.0 passer rating) starting opposite Mansoor Delane (rookie) and L'Jarius Sneed (2025: 60.9% catch rate and 139.3 passer rating). Sutton is a solid flex/WR3 for Week 1 who could easily be a WR2.

Last year, Trevor Lawrence finally had the breakout season that everyone had been waiting for as the QB6 in fantasy points per game. It was the first season in which he had eclipsed 18 fantasy points per game. Yes, part of this magical season included nine rushing touchdowns, which is probably not a sustainable mark to expect him to repeat in 2026, but he was fifth in red zone carries per game among quarterbacks, so maybe there is some carryover in his rushing touchdown production to this season. Lawrence really caught fire to close last season (Weeks 12-18) as the QB1 in fantasy points per game. During that seven-game stretch, among 30 qualifying quarterbacks, Lawrence was excellent as a passer, ranking third in yards per attempt, fifth in passing yards per game, third in hero throw rate, 11th in catchable target rate, and second in passing touchdowns. The Browns lost Myles Garrett during the offseason, but they added Jared Verse. I know it's a downgrade, but not by a ton. Cleveland's pass defense was stout to close last season and could be again in 2026. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, they allowed the seventh-fewest yards per attempt, the 11th-lowest passing success rate, and the third-lowest EPA per dropback. Lawrence could rise above a tough on-paper matchup for Week 1, but it's ok if you have some worries.

Last year, Aaron Jones missed five games while dealing with hamstring, shoulder, and hip injuries. When he was active, he averaged 13.3 touches and 62.3 total yards as the RB31 in fantasy points per game. Entering his age-32 season, I don't think Jones can be expected to play a full 17 games as a workhorse back. He will likely split work with Jordan Mason this season, picking up most of the passing game usage. On early downs, his best days are behind him, as he was 32nd in explosive run rate, 43rd in missed tackle rate, and 49th in yards after contact per attempt. In the receiving game, he is still above average, ranking 26th in yards per route run and 24th in first downs per route run. Jones is only a middling flex to open the 2026 season against his former team. Last year, Green Bay allowed the sixth-lowest explosive run rate and the fifth-fewest yards after contact per attempt while ranking 15th in yards before contact per attempt and rushing success rate allowed.

Last year, in Weeks 13-18, with Brian Thomas Jr. back in the lineup, Parker Washington doing his thing, and Trevor Lawrence playing with his hair on fire, Jakobi Meyers was the WR28 in fantasy points per game. During that six-game stretch, he was seeing a 22.6% target share and a 26.7% first-read share, producing 54.7 receiving yards per game, 1.62 yards per route run, and 0.094 first downs per route run. Meyers will be a solid WR3/flex at times this season, but that won't include Week 1. Last year, when Tyson Campbell and Denzel Ward were on the field together as full-time players, the Cleveland pass defense was a shutdown unit against perimeter wide receivers. In their eight games together, the Browns' pass defense allowed only 1.43 fantasy points per target and 7.24 yards per target to perimeter wide receivers. Over the entire season, those would have been the third-lowest marks in each category in the NFL. Sit Meyers this week.

injury.comment: As expected, Meyers carries no injury designation ahead of Sunday's season opener and will be available to play against the Browns. His presence is further competition for Parker Washington and Brian Thomas Jr. in a crowded Jacksonville WR room.

news.title: Jakobi Meyers (thumb) good to go for Sunday

fp.note: Over the last two seasons, with Bucky Irving in town, Rachaad White was a more effective per-touch player, but with Irving out of the lineup last year, he proved again that he can carry the mail (although while being horribly inefficient). Last season, in Weeks 5-12, White averaged 14.6 touches and 60 total yards while seeing 71% of the snaps. During that span, White was the RB23 in fantasy points per game with a 1.2% explosive run rate, a 14% missed tackle rate, and only 1.52 yards after contact per attempt. White should be operating in a committee this season with Jacory Croskey-Merritt. Behind Washington's suspect offensive line, I don't know how much running room he'll find in Week 1. I'm sitting him in most leagues where I roster him. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Philly allowed the 11th-lowest rushing success rate, the 11th-fewest yards before contact per attempt, and had the ninth-best stuff rate.

Last year, after becoming a Seahawk, Rashid Shaheed had only a 61.9% route share, an 8.8% target share with 20.9 receiving yards per game, 1.05 yards per route run, and a 12.3% first-read share. This type of usage isn't conducive to fantasy success. Yes, could it trend upward in 2026 with a full offseason to learn the ropes? Sure, but that doesn't mean that I'm rushing to plug Shaheed into a flex spot to open the season. Last season, New England utilized single high with 51.8% of their defensive snaps. Against single-high with Seattle, Shaheed posted only an 11% target-per-route run rate and 0.74 yards per route run. Last year, against perimeter wide receivers, New England was 15th in yards per target and 18th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed. Those aren't horrible numbers for Shaheed, but I'm sitting him until we see what his usage looks like for 2026.

Keaton Mitchell will be Omarion Hampton's running mate in the backfield in 2026. We'll still have to see how much usage/volume he'll see on a weekly basis, but he could negate those concerns with his big-play ability as a deep league flex in Week 1. Last season, he had only 68 touches, but he had a 10.2% explosive run rate and a respectable 1.37 yards per route run. Last year, Arizona allowed the third-highest explosive run rate, the fifth-highest rushing success rate, and the 12th-most yards before contact per attempt.

injury.comment: Mitchell has been dealing with a nagging hamstring injury for a while, but it appears he is finally over it, as he has received full clearance to suit up and play for the Chargers in their season opener. He will remain relegated to a depth role behind Omarion Hampton for the foreseeable future, however.

news.title: Keaton Mitchell (hamstring) off injury report for Sunday

fp.note: C.J. Stroud had another struggle bus season last year as the QB20 in fantasy points per game. He had only four weeks in which he cracked the top 12 in weekly scoring among quarterbacks. Among 38 qualifying quarterbacks, he ranked 15th in yards per attempt, 18th in passing yards per game, 28th in highly accurate throw rate, 31st in catchable target rate, and 28th in hero throw rate. Houston tried to hide him, as he had only five games last year with 35 or more passing attempts. I expect the Texans to lean on their defense and run game this week to hopefully take down the Bills. Stroud is a middling QB2. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Buffalo allowed the fewest yards per attempt, the sixth-lowest passer rating, and the eighth-lowest passing success rate.

Last year, AJ Barner was the TE20 in fantasy points per game while finishing as a TE1 in weekly scoring six times. Last year, among 54 qualifying tight ends, he was 27th in target share, 25th in receiving yards per game, 26th in yards per route run, 33rd in first-read share, and 26th in first downs per route run. Last year, he was fifth in total touchdowns among tight ends while also ranking 12th in red zone targets. Barner will have streamable moments in 2026, but this isn't a week where it's likely worth going this direction for your fantasy lineups. Last year, New England allowed the 14th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity while ranking 15th in yards per target permitted to tight ends.

Rashee Rice had another "interesting offseason" where he had a knee scope and spent some time rehabbing from that procedure in a jail cell. Rice hasn't played more than eight games in a season since 2023, so while he has been very productive when he's been on the field over the last two seasons, we still haven't seen him available for a full calendar of football since that season. Last year, when he was on the field, Rice remained a target hog with a 26.2% target share (12th among 109 qualifying receivers), averaging 71.4 receiving yards per game (tenth), producing 2.28 yards per route run (15th), and churning out 0.112 first downs per route run with a 31.9% first-read share (both 14th-best). Rice could see a heavy workload in Week 1, but I don't know that he'll have a ton of productivity with it against a secondary that allowed the second-fewest yards per target and the fewest fantasy points per opportunity to wide receivers last season.

Bhayshul Tuten will compete with Chris Rodriguez to be the lead back for the Jaguars in 2026. I want to bet on Tuten this year and his talent. Last year, Tuten was unfortunately robbed of the stretch run of his rookie season as he was sidelined by a finger injury. Before the injury, he was starting to make some noise. This could be the big breakout season for Tuten, who, on a per-touch basis, flashed the immense talent that I really liked when he was in college. Last season, among 55 qualifying backs, he ranked fifth in rushing success rate, 11th in missed tackle rate, and 17th in yards after contact per attempt. Rodriguez will remain a worry for Tuten at the goal line and for his overall touch count until we see his role fleshed out this season. That uncertainty makes it tough to count on Tuten as an RB2 in Week 1. He could ultimately produce like one this week, but it's tough to project that at the moment. The Browns should field a solid run defense again this season. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Cleveland allowed the 11th-lowest explosive run rate, the 12th-lowest rushing success rate, and the 11th-lowest missed tackle rate.

Terry McLaurin experienced a steep drop-off last year after his banner WR14 campaign in 2024. Ultimately, the Washington offense took a massive step back, and McLaurin was dealing with a quad injury for much of last season, which limited him to ten games played. In those ten games, yes, he was the WR33 in fantasy points per game, but his per-route metrics remained stellar. Among 109 qualifying receivers, McLaurin ranked 25th in target per route run rate (24%), 13th in yards per route run (2.38), fourth in first downs per route run (0.135), and 26th in route win rate. Last year in Washington's two meetings with Philly, the Eagles utilized two high with 60.4% of their defensive snaps. Last year, against two high, McLaurin had only a 20% target-per-route run rate, but he also had 2.26 yards per route run. McLaurin should see plenty of volume this week against Philly, but I worry about his ceiling against this talented secondary. Last year, Philly allowed the third-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Rhamondre Stevenson was the Pats' lead back last year as the RB21 in fantasy points per game, and I don't see that changing in 2026. Stevenson was amazing on a per-touch basis, and he bested TreVeyon Henderson in EVERY discernible metric that I care about. Last year, Stevenson was fifth in explosive run rate, missed tackle rate, and yards after contact per attempt (per Fantasy Points Data). Stevenson also surpassed Henderson in yards per route run (1.41 vs. 0.98) and pass protection. Unless Stevenson falls off in 2026, he should remain the lead back for New England after playing at least 57% of the snaps in nine of his 14 games played in 2025. Stevenson should have a productive day, but it won't be easy sledding in the rushing department. Last year, Seattle allowed the lowest explosive run rate, the fifth-lowest rushing success rate, and had the fifth-highest stuff rate. Stevenson will have to get it done as a receiver, which he should be able to. Last year, among 52 qualifying backs, Stevenson ranked 15th in yards per route run and first in yards per target. Seattle allowed backs to "run through the air" all season, giving up the eighth-most receiving fantasy points per game, the ninth-most receiving yards, and the most receptions to the position.

Last year, Jake Ferguson managed his second TE10 finish in fantasy points per game among tight ends in the last three years. Last year, among 54 qualifying tight ends, Ferguson was 16th in target share (16%), 20th in receiving yards per game (35.3), 43rd in yards per route run (1.26), 18th in first-read share (17.6%), and 38th in first downs per route run. What fueled his season was red zone targets (second among tight ends behind only Trey McBride) and touchdowns (tied for third-best). I expect Ferguson to be a consistent red zone weapon for Dak Prescott again in 2026. With his touchdown equity alone, Ferguson could be a TE1 in Week 1. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, the Giants allowed the most yards per target and the 14th-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

MarShawn Lloyd looks primed to enter Week 1 as the Packers' workhorse back with Josh Jacobs on the commissioner-exempt list. Just to remind everyone about Lloyd's talent. During his final two collegiate seasons, he was 20th and 16th in yards after contact per attempt, third and 18th in breakaway rate, and fourth and 15th in elusive rating (per PFF, minimum 100 carries). Lloyd can take advantage of a run defense that lost some parts but added Caleb Banks, Domonique Orange, and Jake Golday this offseason. Minnesota could field an improved run defense in 2026, but I have to see it to believe it at this point. Last year, Minny ranked 16th in explosive run rate and 15th in yards after contact per attempt while giving up the sixth-highest rushing success rate and the fourth-lowest stuff rate.

Last year, after taking over as the Giants' starter, Jaxson Dart was the QB7 in fantasy points per game. If you remove the wet fart game that he had in Week 16 against Minnesota, where he scored only one fantasy point and had 13 pass attempts and 33 passing yards, he averaged 22.5 fantasy points per game. That points-per-game mark would have made him the QB1 in fantasy points per game last year. Dart showed off his rushing ability, averaging seven rushing attempts and 40.6 rushing yards per game. He had the second-most rushing yards per game among quarterbacks last year, behind only Justin Fields. Dart also wasn't a lackluster passer last year. Among 38 qualifying passers, he was 23rd in CPOE, 19th in highly accurate throw rate, and tenth in hero throw rate. Dart was also fifth in fantasy points per dropback while dealing with the 12th-highest drop rate among quarterbacks. The Giants' second-year signal-caller will face a revamped Dallas pass defense that added Rashan Gary, Cobie Durant, Jalen Thompson, and Caleb Downs this offseason. They'll be a much improved unit for 2026, but the question is how much? Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Dallas's pass defense was almost non-existent as they allowed the most fantasy points per dropback, the second-most yards per attempt, and the fifth-highest CPOE. Dallas should be viewed at least as a league-average matchup for Dart, with the upside to be a very good one.

I can't wait to see Malik Willis in his first start for the Dolphins. I know the starting resume for Willis is limited. I get it. What we have seen in limited doses over the last two years has been outstanding, though. Over the last two seasons, Willis has posted a 5.6% big-time throw rate (118 dropbacks, per PFF), 10.9 yards per attempt, and averaged 44.8 rushing yards per game. Last year, among all quarterbacks with at least 110 dropbacks, that big-time throw rate would have ranked eighth-best behind Caleb Williams, and his yards per attempt mark would have led the NFL. That rushing yardage mark per game over the last three years would have ranked first, fourth, and third among quarterbacks. Willis is facing a remade Raiders' defense that added Quay Walker, Kwity Paye, Nakobe Dean, and Taron Johnson (just to name a few). Last year, the Raiders allowed the tenth-highest passer rating, the ninth-highest passing success rate, and the tenth-highest EPA per dropback. I don't know if the Raiders' pass defense will be that much of a pushover in 2026, but I also don't know if they hit the ground running immediately out of the gate. Willis' rushing ability gives him an incredibly high ceiling and floor for Week 1.

Ja'Kobi Lane was the talk of training camp and preseason football. He could easily be a late-round dart from fantasy draft season that hits in 2026, with a clear path to targets for a talented receiver behind Zay Flowers. Mark Andrews is a giant question mark, and Rashod Bateman has off-field issues that could lead to a suspension. During his final collegiate season, Lane ranked 52nd in yards per route run and 27th in receiving grade (per PFF). Lane could have a solid role in Week 1, but I'm not running him out there in Week 1 unless I'm in a deep league or dynasty league where I'm lacking better options. Last year, Indy allowed the ninth-fewest yards per target and ranked 15th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to perimeter wide receivers.

injury.comment: Lane was seeing some promising usage before exiting with his injury, having a touchdown nullified by holding, another endzone target just out of his reach, and an 11-yard gain on his one reception. The Ravens are now short on receivers unless Zay Flowers, who also exited with an injury, can come back for next week's game. In his absence, expect more work for Rashod Bateman, Chris Moore, and potentially fellow rookie Elijah Sarratt.

news.title: Ja'Kobi Lane (wrist) out for several weeks with broken wrist

fp.note: Ashton Jeanty is dealing with a sprained ankle, but he practiced in full all week. He doesn't carry an injury designation into Week 1, so I'm expecting him to get a full workload to open the season. Ashton Jeanty was seen as a disappointment for fantasy managers exiting his rookie season. It wasn't a failure, but you can make the argument that, because of his talent and the hype, it didn't live up to lofty expectations. Jeanty was the RB15 in fantasy points per game, finishing with 321 touches and 1,321 total yards. He ranked fifth in snap share, first in opportunity share, seventh in weighted opportunities, and 15th in red zone touches. Among 49 qualifying backs, Jeanty ranked 16th in missed tackle rate and 17th in yards after contact per attempt. The ecosystem surrounding Jeanty stunk. The Raiders were 31st in red zone scoring attempts per game and 30th in yards per play. Among those 49 qualifying backs previously, Jeanty had the second-fewest yards before contact per attempt (1.28), and 65% of his rushing yards came after first contact. With Klint Kubiak in town and (hopefully) improved blocking up front, Jeanty could have a nice Week 1. Last year, the Dolphins allowed the fifth-highest explosive run rate, the most yards after contact per attempt, and the sixth-highest missed tackle rate. Even with the best rose colored glasses, this still has to be viewed as an above-average matchup for the Raiders' ground game.

injury.comment: Jeanty practiced in full all week. He should be good to go in his lead role to open the season.

news.title: Ashton Jeanty (ankle) off injury report Sunday

fp.note: Last year was a disappointing season for Ladd McConkey. He finished as the WR34 in fantasy points per game, with eight weeks outside the top 36 wide receivers in weekly scoring. The hype was heavy in draft season for McConkey to post monster numbers in Mike McDaniel's offense. I love McConkey's talent, but found myself lower than the market and expectations for McConkey this season. Last year, among 109 qualifying receivers, he ranked 41st in separation and 15th in route win rate. Those aren't damning numbers at all. Last year, among the same subset of receivers, McConkey was 29th in target share (19.8%), 62nd in yards per route run (1.47), 37th in receiving yards per game (49.3), 46th in first-read share (20.4%), and 64th in first downs per route run. None of that screams "amazing WR2 for fantasy purposes with WR1 upside." Last year, Arizona was 16th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to wide receivers. McConkey should be in fantasy lineups in Week 1 with a middling matchup on deck.

news.title: Ladd McConkey (undisclosed) exits early Sunday

fp.note: Last year, Tetairoa McMillan had a strong rookie season as the WR20 in fantasy points per game despite a limited passing-volume offense and up-and-down quarterback play from Bryce Young. Last year, in Weeks 3-18, Young surpassed 35 passing attempts only once, had only two games with more than 225 passing yards, and directed an offense that was fifth in neutral rushing rate. Last year, McMillan, among 109 qualifying receivers, ranked 14th in target share (23.1%), 19th in receiving yards per game (59.6), 27th in yards per route run (1.94), 15th in first-read share (28.5%), and 17th in first downs per route run (0.105). Last year, to close the season in Weeks 17-20, Chicago leaned into single high coverage as a pass defense (58.2%). McMillan was excellent against single-high last year with a 26% target-per-route run rate and 2.06 yards per route run. McMillan could easily begin the season with a standout Week 1. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Chicago allowed the second-most yards per target and the fifth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

It seems like George Kittle will be ready to rock for Week 1. Now, if he's active, will he play a full-time role for the 49ers? I doubt it, but he could still easily have a 50-60% snap rate and be heavily involved when they are passing and around the goal line. When Kittle was on the field last year, he didn't show any signs of slowing down. Among 54 qualifying tight ends, he ranked fourth in target share (20%) and yards per route run (2.30), third in receiving yards per game (57.1) and first-read share (24.3%), and second in first downs per route run (0.139). Kittle could have another amazing season in 2026 for fantasy, but I'm willing to sit him in Week 1 with the playing time concerns and a tough matchup. Last year, the Rams allowed the third-fewest yards per target and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Well, Carnell Tate didn't have a banner preseason as he failed to secure any of his six targets, but I don't put this slow start on Tate. I think it rests at the feet of Cam Ward. I'm not fading Tate's talent off a small 25-route preseason sample. Tate displayed in college that he's an amazing route runner who can separate at all three levels of the field after ranking tenth in yards per route run and fourth in receiving grade last season (per PFF). He finished college with an otherworldly 68.8% contested catch rate, and he had zero drops in his final season despite a 14.6 aDOT. The outside corner tandem of Brandon Stephens (2025: 67.1% catch rate and 126.4 passer rating) and Nashon Wright (2025: 64.5% catch rate and 98.0 passer rating) doesn't strike fear in my heart. Tate could walk away from Week 1 with a wonderful stat line that has everyone reconsidering their offseason fade of him. It all comes down to Cam Ward and his ability to get Tate catchable targets.

Patrick Mahomes saw his season end in Week 15 last year with a torn ACL. Prior to that horrible injury, he was the QB2 in fantasy points per game. Last year, he averaged a career-high 6.6 rushing attempts per game and 30.1 rushing yards per game. He was first in scrambles per game and 14th in red zone carries per game among quarterbacks. I don't expect those numbers to repeat this season coming off the ACL injury. Mahomes will work from the pocket more in 2026, especially to open the season. Last year, outside of the immense passing volume he saw, it was an uninspiring year for Mahomes as an accurate passer. Among 38 qualifying passers, he was 18th in yards per attempt, 24th in adjusted completion rate, 16th in highly accurate throw rate, and 30th in catchable target rate. Denver is a tough test out of the gate for Mahomes. Last year, Denver allowed the second-fewest yards per attempt, the sixth-lowest passer rating, the second-lowest passing success rate, and the sixth-fewest EPA per dropback.

J.K. Dobbins should be Denver's early down hammer again this year. Last year, in Weeks 1-10, he was the RB24 in fantasy points per game, averaging 16.4 touches and 80.6 total yards. The bulk of that work was in the rushing department, as he averaged only 1.4 targets and 3.7 receiving yards per game. He had only four games in which he saw more than one target, and he never saw more than two targets in any game. Dobbins was on pace for 260 carries and 1,313 rushing yards before his injury, so his value on early downs is quite nice. Among 49 qualifying backs, he ranked third in explosive run rate and eighth in missed tackle rate. Dobbins should have a productive Week 1 against a run defense that last year allowed the eighth-highest zone rushing success rate (Dobbins 54.9% zone in 2025), had the tenth-lowest rate of hits at or behind the line of scrimmage, and ranked 17th in yards before contact per attempt.

KC Concepcion has the talent to be Cleveland's clear WR1 this season. We'll see if that's how it shakes out this season. Concepcion is a receiver who can threaten a defense at all three levels while also making things happen after the catch with the ball in his hands. In two of his last three collegiate seasons, he ranked top 35 in FBS in YAC per reception (26th, 33rd, per PFF). In 2023, Concepcion was 17th in missed tackles forced among FBS wide receivers. Concepcion won't have easy sledding in his first NFL game, though. Last year, Jacksonville allowed the second-fewest fantasy points per target and the third-fewest yards per target to slot receivers.

Mike Washington Jr. could offer nice flex value in Week 1. Washington Jr. could see double-digit touches with the ability to break off a long run for a score at any time. He has looked amazing this preseason with an every-down skillset. Washington Jr. tested like an alien during the pre-draft process, leading to his fourth-round draft capital. During his final collegiate season, Washington Jr. broke out, ranking 33rd in yards after contact per attempt and 17th in breakaway rate (per PFF). Last year, the Dolphins allowed the fifth-highest explosive run rate, the most yards after contact per attempt, and the sixth-highest missed tackle rate. Even with the best rose colored glasses, this still has to be viewed as an above-average matchup for the Raiders' ground game.

news.title: Kenyon Sadiq (groin) without injury designation for Sunday

fp.note: Dontayvion Wicks has been a separation-score and route-win-rate darling over the last two years, and could finally step into a bigger role this year in Philly. Over the last two years, Wicks has ranked third and 24th in separation score and sixth and seventh in route win rate among all wide receivers with at least 200 routes. Last year, Wicks posted a 21% target-per-route run rate, 1.56 yards per route run, and 0.099 first downs per route run. Among 109 qualifying receivers, Wicks ranked 41st in target-per-route run rate and 25th in first downs per route run. Washington added Rasul Douglas (2025: 56.8% catch rate and 75.2 passer rating) to the perimeter corner mix this offseason. We'll see if he can be a big upgrade to a unit that allowed the sixth-most fantasy points per target and the third-highest passer rating to perimeter wide receivers last season.

Cam Ward had a rough rookie season, but he was also airdropped into a horrible situation. Calvin Ridley was the only dependable receiver that he had entering the season, and he was limited to only seven games played. Ward was the QB33 in fantasy points per game with only one week as a QB1 in weekly scoring. Even when Ward's play improved marginally in Weeks 12-18, it wasn't amazing. During that stretch, among 30 qualifying passers, he was 15th in adjusted completion rate, 22nd in highly accurate throw rate, 26th in catchable target rate, and 23rd in hero throw rate. Tennessee added Wan'Dale Robinson and Carnell Tate during the offseason to spruce up this passing attack and give Ward a fighting chance at a breakout season. During the preseason, it didn't look promising, but it's an incredibly small sample. In preseason action, among 62 qualifying quarterbacks, Ward ranked 46th in yards per attempt, 38th in adjusted completion rate, and 54th in aDOT. The Jets are another defense that added a ton of talent this offseason with the additions of T'Vondre Sweat, David Bailey, Demario Davis, Nashon Wright, and Minkah Fitzpatrick. We'll see how quickly all of these new parts and pieces can gel this season, but the Jets should be an improved pass defense. Last year, New York allowed the eighth-most yards per attempt, the highest passer rating, and the 11th-highest success rate. At the very least, this should be viewed as an above-average matchup for Ward to open the season.

Injuries crushed Jayden Daniels' 2025 season. Daniels dealt with a knee sprain, a right hamstring injury, a dislocated elbow, and an elbow sprain. Daniels still managed to flash the upside in his four full games played last year to remind people why they fell in love with him in the first place. In those four games, Daniels averaged 20.2 fantasy points per game, nine rushing attempts, and 44 yards on the ground. If he had kept up that pace all season, he would have been the QB7 in fantasy points per game and averaged the second-most rushing yards per game among quarterbacks. With all of the injuries he sustained last year, his stats are a muddied mess that are better off tossed in the trash, but for the sake of doing my due diligence among 45 qualifying quarterbacks, he ranked 42nd in highly accurate throw rate, 38th in catchable target rate, and 25th in hero throw rate. Daniels' rushing ability will have to carry his Week 1 fantasy production because he'll be under duress when dropping back to throw against one of the best pass defenses in the NFL. Last year, Philly was fifth in pressure rate while allowing the sixth-fewest yards per attempt, the second-lowest passer rating, and the third-lowest passing success rate. I hope Washington's patchwork offensive line can give him time to throw, but I have my concerns.

I don't want to read too much into the preseason usage for the Titans' backfield. Brian Daboll has a long history of utilizing one workhorse back in his offenses, so I'm still projecting Tony Pollard to be that guy. Could I be wrong and this is a 50/50 committee? Yep. Last year, Pollard ranked 15th in snap share, 17th in opportunity share, and 16th in weighted opportunities, but because of the putrid offensive situation he found himself in, he was only the RB29 in fantasy points per game. This can be traced to his five total touchdowns, which were a result of an offense that was 30th in points per game and 32nd in red zone scoring attempts per game, so it makes sense that he also ranked 49th in red zone touches. Pollard was still solid on a per-touch basis. Among 49 qualifying backs, he ranked 25th in explosive run rate and 22nd in yards after contact per attempt. The Jets added defensive firepower to their defensive line and linebacker room this offseason, so I project that their run defense will take another step forward in 2026. They were already a strong unit last season. Last year, New York allowed the sixth-lowest rushing success rate, the sixth-fewest yards before contact per attempt, and had the tenth-highest hit rate at or behind the line of scrimmage. Pollard is hopefully a volume play with RB2 upside in Week 1.

Christian Watson got the bag this offseason and should be considered the clear WR1 for the Green Bay Packers. Watson deserved the payday as he proved that he can handle this role last year. Last season, in Weeks 8-18, he was the WR21 in fantasy points per game with an 18.2% target share, 61.1 receiving yards per game, 2.67 yards per route run, a 23.9% first-read share, and 0.122 first downs per route run. His target share and first-read share should go up this season with Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks gone and Watson likely getting promoted into a full-time role. Last year, he was also held back by a 68% route share (56th out of 109 qualifying receivers). Jordan Love will be blitzed incessantly this week by Brian Flores, but that should work in Watson's favor. Last year, when Love was blitzed, Watson was tied for the team lead with a 26% target-per-route run rate while ranking second with a 21% first-read share and posting 2.60 yards per route run. Last year, Minny allowed the second-most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers. I expect Watson to shine in Week 1.

Isaiah Likely's 2025 season was crushed by a foot injury that he sustained in the preseason. I can't honestly tell you whether he was fully healthy last season or when that occurred, if so. I'm tossing his 2025 campaign in the trash. So, let's be kind and rewind to 2024. During that season, among 57 qualifying tight ends, Likely ranked 17th in target per route run rate, tenth in yards per route run, and eighth in first downs per route run and fantasy points per route run. After signing a lucrative deal with the Giants this offseason, Likely should be their clear starting tight end and a strong part of their passing game. I expect Likely to open the season as the second option in the passing game behind only Malik Nabers. The Dallas secondary has been overhauled this offseason, but it's worth noting that in Weeks 12-18 last year, this defense allowed the fourth-most yards per target and the fifth-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends. Likely could easily be a strong TE1 in Week 1.

I'm curious what Makai Lemon's role will be out of the gate for Philly in 2026 after missing substantial parts of rookie camp, training camp, and the preseason. Lemon played on the perimeter with 71.4% of his snaps in his limited preseason action, but I doubt that will be the case when he's on the field with DeVonta Smith and Dontayvioin Wicks. Lemon finished a productive collegiate career ranking sixth and 12th in yards per route run, ninth and 50th in missed tackles forced, and 60th and 28th in YAC per reception over the last two seasons (per PFF). I expect Lemon to be the team's starting slot receiver to begin the season, and I wouldn't be surprised if he has a limited snap role if Philly looks to deploy 12 and 21 personnel heavily out of the gate. Lemon could have a solid fantasy day in Week 1, despite the risks that I outlined here. Washington couldn't stop slot receivers last year, allowing the seventh-highest passer rating and the most fantasy points per target to the position. Lemon is a decent flex play for Week 1.

Daniel Jones' monster 2025 season was derailed by a fractured fibula (Week 12) and then a season-ending ruptured Achilles (Week 14). In Weeks 1-10, when Jones was healthy, among 37 qualifying quarterbacks, he ranked fourth in yards per attempt, 15th in adjusted completion rate, ninth in highly accurate throw rate, and 17th in hero throw rate. During that stretch, he was the QB9 in fantasy points per game, contributing 14.3 rushing yards per game (five rushing touchdowns). Jones did fall off in his final three games played last year, which could be the league catching up to the Colts' offense, or it could also be injuries taking a toll on him. Last year, the Ravens' pass defense was in shambles. The addition of defensive mastermind Jesse Minter should help this defense rebound in 2026, but will it be elite immediately from the jump? We shall see. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Baltimore allowed the 12th-most yards per attempt, the most passing yards per game, and the ninth-highest passing success rate, but again I'd take these numbers with a grain of salt. With Jones still likely rounding into form off the Achilles to begin the season and Baltimore's defense with a sharp coach at the controls this year, I'm more worried about Jones in Week 1 than the numbers might suggest I should be.

Last year, Bo Nix regressed as a passer, and with his overall production, he was still the QB11 in fantasy points per game. Nix saw his passing touchdown rate fall from 5.1% to 4.1%, and his rushing yards per game dip from 25.3 to 20.9 (16th). Nix still directed a passing offense that was fifth in neutral passing rate and tenth in neutral pace. I don't see either of those figures changing in 2026. If anything, Denver could easily be top five in neutral pace this season with all of the news coming out of the Broncos' camp this offseason about new playcaller Davis Webb. Among 38 qualifying passers, he was 31st in yards per attempt, 18th in highly accurate throw rate, 19th in hero throw rate, and 22nd in fantasy points per dropback. Last year, in his two regular season meetings with Kansas City, Nix was the QB19 and QB10 in weekly fantasy scoring. He could easily be a QB1 this week against a pass defense that allowed the 13th-highest passer rating last year while ranking 19th in passing success rate and 18th in EPA per dropback allowed.

I'm not buying the offseason narratives that the Texans backfield will be a 50/50 split. David Montgomery will likely operate as the team's workhorse. Last year, he was phased out of the Lions' offensive plans as the season moved along, which led to his RB32 finish in fantasy points per game. In Weeks 12-18, he was the RB43 in fantasy points per game with a 32.1% snap rate, 8.2 touches per game, and only 42.8 total yards per game. Montgomery still has the juice to produce as a workhorse this season. Last season, he ranked 30th in missed tackle rate, but he was 12th in yards after contact per attempt. His receiving chops are also still alive and well, as he was also 22nd in yards per route run and 12th in first downs per route run. Last season, Montgomery bested Marks in explosive run rate, missed tackle rate, rushing success rate, yards after contact per attempt, and yards per route run. Legit, every per-touch metric that I care about. Montgomery is the superior back, even at this stage of his career. Montgomery should have a successful Week 1 against a run defense that last season (in Weeks 12-18) allowed the 13th-highest rushing success rate, the 14th-highest yards before contact per attempt, and had the 11th-lowest stuff rate.

Parker Washington finished last season with a flurry of insane production; if he picks up right where he left off, he'll crush this season. Last year, in Weeks 16-19, Washington asserted himself as the Jags' clear WR1. During that stretch, he averaged 22.3 PPR points per game while soaking up six red zone targets and 13 deep targets. In those four games, he had a 28.9% target share, 113.5 receiving yards per game, 3.78 yards per route run, and a 33.3% first-read share. Those are all absolutely elite metrics no matter how you slice it. I have no concern about Parker Washington's ability to get open this week against Cleveland's slot corner, Myles Harden (2025: 71.9% catch rate and 119.3 passer rating). Last year, among 34 qualifying slot corners, Harden allowed the fifth-highest passer rating, the ninth-most fantasy points per target, and the ninth-highest rate of a step of separation.

Mark Andrews is coming off his worst season in the NFL as the TE23 in fantasy points per game. Last year, Baltimore limited his playing time, as he was 22nd in route share (62.9%, per Fantasy Points Data). I'm expecting that to rebound in 2026 with Isaiah Likely gone, but we still have to see it materialize. Last year, among 59 qualifying tight ends, Andrews was ninth in first-read share, but his yards per route run (41st) and first downs per route run (27th) were nothing to write home about. Andrews could have a nice game in Week 1 that quells some of my concerns about his 2026 season. Last year, Indy allowed the fourth-most yards per target and the 12th-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends. Lou Anarumo's defenses have bled out production to tight ends over the years, so this wasn't a one-year isolated incident. I think it transfers over to 2026.

Last year, Xavier Worthy finished as the WR54 in fantasy points per game with only one week as a top-24 wide receiver in weekly scoring. Last year, after returning from a shoulder injury (Weeks 4-17), he only had a 15.8% target share, 1.40 yards per route run, 40.9 receiving yards per game, a 19.5% first-read share, 0.058 first downs per route run, and 8.5 PPR points per game. Sit Worthy in Week 1 against a secondary that allowed the second-fewest yards per target and the fewest fantasy points per opportunity to wide receivers last season.

news.title: Alvin Kamara (knee) inactive for Week 1

fp.note: Bryce Young didn't take the fantasy leap that we all hoped for last year. He finished the season as the QB24 in fantasy points per game with only five games as a QB1 in weekly scoring. The rushing floor I was hoping we would get in 2025 after some glimpses in 2024 also wasn't there, as he surpassed 25 rushing yards in only three games. Carolina tried to hide him as he surpassed 225 passing yards only three times and had more than 30 passing attempts only five times. Despite all of this, Young could post a solid QB2 stat line this week. Chicago's pass defense (outside of the turnovers) was dreadful last year. In Weeks 12-18 last season, the Bears allowed the 13th-most yards per attempt, the ninth-most passing touchdowns, and the tenth-highest passing success rate.

Jaylen Waddle should be Denver's unquestioned WR1 this season. Last year, among 109 qualifying wide receivers, he was 12th in target per route run rate, 12th in yards per route run, seventh in first downs per route run, 12th in separation score, and 11th in route win rate. He also bested Courtland Sutton in each of those metrics with the exception of route win rate (15.3% vs. 15.5%). We'll see how quickly the new (or throwback, depending on how you choose to view it) look Kansas City corner room can hit the ground running with Nohl Williams (2025: 52.6% catch rate and 85.0 passer rating) starting opposite Mansoor Delane (rookie) and L'Jarius Sneed (2025: 60.9% catch rate and 139.3 passer rating). Waddle should be heavily involved Week 1.

Last year, Kyle Pitts had a tale of two seasons. Yes, overall it was a wonderful year as the TE5 in fantasy points per game and easily his best statistical season since his rookie year, but it was wildly different with Drake London in and out of the lineup. Without London, Pitts had a 26.7% target share with 84.4 receiving yards per game, 2.81 yards per route run, a 27.8% first-read share, 0.120 first downs per route run, and 19 fantasy points per game. Those are all elite numbers, and if Pitts had put up those stats all year, especially the fantasy points per game, he would have been the TE1 for fantasy. The problem is that with Drake London active, Pitts had a 19% target share, 42.2 receiving yards per game, 1.43 yards per route run, a 20.2% first-read share, 0.093 first downs per route run, and 9.6 fantasy points per game. All of those per-route metrics were still quite strong, but the fantasy points per game mark would have made Pitts the TE20 last year. London will be on the field for Week 1, and now Kyle Pitts has to deal with the quarterbacking rollercoaster of Cooper Rush. The small ray of hope for Pitts in Week 1 is that Pittsburgh struggled to defend tight ends to close last season, but they added Jaquan Brisker to the secondary this offseason. Maybe Brisker can help improve their defense against tight ends, but at the moment that's just a hopeful projection. Pitts will have to overcome London's target-hogging presence and Cooper Rush in Week 1 to post a solid stat line. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Pittsburgh allowed the 12th-most yards per target and the sixth-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Last season, Jaylen Warren had arguably his most productive season for fantasy purposes as the RB18 in fantasy points per game. He was his usual incredibly efficient self on a per-touch basis. In 2025, Warren ranked sixth in missed tackle rate, ninth in yards after contact per attempt, 12th in rushing success rate, third in yards per route run, and seventh in first downs per route run. He set career highs in carries (211), rushing yards (958), and total touchdowns (eight). Kenneth Gainwell moved on from Pittsburgh in the offseason, but Mike McCarthy brought in his favorite son, Rico Dowdle. Warren's role for Pittsburgh has evolved over the years from preferred passing-down back to lead back, but his role could be in flux in 2026 with the arrival of a new head coach and backfield mate. Warren can't be counted on for more than a flex play for Week 1, with his usage up in the air. If Warren does get into the end zone in Week 1, he could easily pay off as a flex, though. Atlanta was a middle-of-the-road run defense last year to close the season. In Weeks 12-18, Atlanta was 15th in stuff rate and rushing success rate allowed while also ranking 16th in yards before contact per attempt.

Last year, as the quarterback play in Minnesota cratered, Jordan Addison had a career-worst season as the WR44 in fantasy points per game. Addison had only a 17.4% target share with 43.6 receiving yards per game, 1.53 yards per route run, a 22.1% first-read share, and 0.065 first downs per route run. None of those numbers jump off the page, but there's hope for Addison's flex value for Week 1. Since 2023, Jonathon Gannon has utilized two high at the third-highest rate (57.6%). During the same stretch of time, against two high, Addison has seen his target-per-route-run rate climb from 18% to 20% and his yards per route run increase from 1.50 to 1.85 against two high. If Kyler Murray can prove me wrong in Week 1, Addison could have a nice game. Last year, Green Bay allowed the ninth-most receiving yards per game and the fifth-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Jayden Reed missed much of the 2025 season with a broken collarbone and surgery to repair a Jones fracture. Last year, we got only a five-game sample for Reed where he played at least 35% of the snaps. In those contests, Reed had a 21% target-per-route-run rate, 1.99 yards per route run, and 0.47 fantasy points per route run. Those are strong numbers, but the worry for Reed persists into 2026 about his inclusion in two wide receiver sets. Last year, Reed played 75% of his snaps from the slot, which is tough when Green Bay ranked 22nd in usage of 11 personnel (55.6%). Sit Reed this week. Last year, Minnesota allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target, the second-fewest receiving yards per game, and the sixth-fewest fantasy points per target to slot receivers.

Deebo Samuel rejoins the San Francisco 49ers on a one-year deal after a one-year dalliance with the Commanders. Last year, Samuel was the WR29 in fantasy points per game while putting up a varied stat line. Last year, among 109 qualifying receivers, Samuel was 18th in target share (22.4%), ninth in yards after the catch per reception (6.6), 21st in first-read share (27.3%), and ninth-best in missed tackles forced per reception. Unfortunately, though, among the same sample of receivers, he was also 38th in yards per route run and 53rd in first downs per route run (0.076) while seeing his usual bevy of underneath targets (5.3 aDOT, 103rd out of 109 qualifying receivers). Last year, the Rams utilized zone coverage at the seventh-highest rate (76.4%). Over the last three seasons, against zone, Samuel has had a 23% target-per-route run rate and 2.06 yards per route run. Samuel is a viable PPR flex for Week 1, but the matchup is tough. Last year, the Rams allowed the 14th-fewest yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to receivers.

Last year, Juwan Johnson finished with a career high in targets, receptions, and receiving yards as the TE11 in fantasy points per game. Last year, among 54 qualifying tight ends, Johnson was 13th in target share, seventh in receiving yards per game, 15th in yards per route run, 11th in first-read share, and 23rd in first downs per route run. Johnson could easily post TE1 numbers in Week 1. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Detroit ranked 15th in yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity allowed to tight ends.

Last year, after joining the Jets, Adonai Mitchell saw a 23.6% target share and a 30% first-read share, but he did very little with it, producing only 37.6 receiving yards per game and 1.37 yards per route run. This preseason, Mitchell saw only two targets, and he had a 13.0 aDOT. I expect him to be the field stretcher for the Jets' passing attack this season. The Titans overhauled their secondary this offseason, but it's worth noting that last year they allowed the fifth-most deep passing yards per game and the second-highest deep adjusted completion rate. Do I think those stats will be sticky and projectable for 2026? Eh. We'll see. I'm not running Mitchell out there in Week 1 in a fantasy lineup unless we're talking about a deep dynasty league where you're scraping the bottom of the barrel.

Tyler Allgeier is a touchdown-dependent flex option for Week 1. Last year, he was the RB45 in fantasy points per game, but with his eight scores last year, he had eight weeks as a top-36 running back and four games as a top-24 option in weekly scoring. Allgeier will be a thorn in Jeremiyah Love's side like he was for Bijan Robinson for a number of seasons. Last year, among 49 qualifying backs, Allgeier was 36th in explosive run rate, 39th in missed tackle rate, and 43rd in yards after contact per attempt. This offseason, the Bolts added Dalvin Tomlinson and Akheem Mesidor to the defensive front, but I don't know if that's enough for their run defense to take a huge leap forward. Last season, the Bolts allowed the eighth-highest explosive run rate, the 11th-highest rushing success rate, and the 13th-most yards before contact per attempt.

Greg Dulcich could challenge for the lead in targets for Miami in Week 1. Ok, that might be a tad aggressive, but this receiving depth chart is questionable at best despite my hope for it. Last year, Dulcich was absolutely awesome when on the field. Among 59 qualifying tight ends, he was fifth in target-per-route-run rate (24%), second in yards per route run (2.64) and yards after the catch per reception (7.69), fifth in first downs per route run (0.110), and sixth in fantasy points per route run. Dulcich could flirt with TE1 production in Week 1 against a secondary that was 15th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed last year against tight ends.

news.title: A.J. Brown (ankle) out at least six weeks

fp.note: Last year was the second time in Dallas Goedert's career that he finished as a top-six fantasy tight end (TE6 in fantasy points per game). Goedert accomplished this by spiking a career-high 11 receiving touchdowns. Last year, among 59 qualifying tight ends, Goedert ranked eighth in target share (18.4%), 33rd in yards per route run (1.43), 17th in receiving yards per game (39.4), eighth in first-read share (21%), seventh in red zone targets (15), and 21st in first downs per route run (0.083). Washington added a lot of firepower to their pass rush and secondary this offseason, but we'll see how much and how quickly they can improve a defense that allowed the most yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends last year.

Yes, D.K. Metcalf finished as the WR19 in fantasy points per game last year, but if you rostered him last season, you know that it wasn't nearly that glorious to trot him out in your lineup weekly. In nine of his 15 games played, he was outside the top 24 receivers in weekly scoring. Last year, among 109 qualifying receivers, Metcalf ranked 24th in target share (21.1%), 26th in receiving yards per game (56.7), 25th in yards per route run (1.98), 20th in first-read share (27.7%), and 37th in first downs per route run. Metcalf's Week 1 matchup does work in his favor, though. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Atlanta had the fourth-highest single-high rate (59.4%). Last year, against single-high, Metcalf had a robust 28% target-per-route-run rate and 2.38 yards per route run. In Weeks 12-18, Atlanta allowed the second-most fantasy points per game and the second-most receiving touchdowns to perimeter wide receivers. Metcalf should lead the way for Pittsburgh's passing attack in Week 1.

Keenan Allen should be a valuable part of the Colts' offense in Week 1. Alec Pierce's playing time and effectiveness are up in the air. Outside of Allen and Pierce, the Colts have only Josh Downs and Tyler Warren to lean on through the air. Last year, Allen proved that he still has gas in the tank on multiple levels as the WR36 in fantasy points per game. Among 109 qualifying receivers, he was 54th in overall separation, 14th in overall route win rate, 22nd in slot yards per route run (2.09), and 18th in route win rate as a perimeter wide receiver. Last year, Allen ran 60.5% of his routes as a perimeter wide receiver while drawing a 20.7% target share with 45.7 receiving yards per game, 1.72 yards per route run, a 24.4% first-read share, and 0.108 first downs per route run. The Ravens should field an improved pass defense this season, but last year their secondary wasn't hopeless against receivers. They allowed the 11th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity and ranked 15th in yards per target. Allen should see enough volume in Week 1 to be a decent flex play.

At this point in his career, we know who Khalil Shakir is. A low-ceiling WR3/4 or flex play on a weekly basis in PPR formats. Over the last two seasons, he has finished as the WR39 and WR33 in fantasy points per game. Last year, among 109 qualifying receivers, Shakir was 36th in target share, 55th in receiving yards per game, 41st in yards per route run, 38th in first-read share, and 80th in first downs per route run. This isn't the week to consider flexing Shakir. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Houston allowed the 11th-fewest fantasy points per game to receiving yards and the tenth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers.

Jordan Mason is a one-trick pony, but that one trick is quite good. He's a strong early-down option for NFL offenses and should continue to serve in the role this season for Minnesota. Last year, he was the RB42 in fantasy points per game while soaking up 158 rushing attempts and producing 758 rushing yards and six total touchdowns. Among 49 qualifying backs, he ranked tenth in explosive run rate, seventh in rushing success rate, ninth in missed tackle rate, and 15th in yards after contact per attempt. Aaron Jones will continue to be the passing-down partner for Mason for Minny in 2026. Mason is a viable touchdown-dependent flex for Week 1. Last year, Green Bay allowed the sixth-lowest explosive run rate and the fifth-fewest yards after contact per attempt while ranking 15th in yards before contact per attempt and rushing success rate allowed.

I'm concerned about Drake London's outlook for Week 1 with Cooper Rush under center. (Please, Jack Strand, save us.) Rush isn't the worst starting quarterback in the NFL for Week 1, but he isn't great, either. Last year, despite Michael Penix and Kirk Cousins, London was cooking last year before a PCL injury derailed his season in Week 11. In Weeks 1-10 last year, London was the WR6 in fantasy points per game. During that stretch, he was fourth in target share (30.3%), fourth in receiving yards per game (86.4), sixth in yards per route run (2.74), fifth in first-read share (37.6%), and seventh in first downs per route run (0.135). Rush isn't even on par with Penix or Cousins as a quarterback; thus lie the concerns for Week 1. The matchup for London also isn't great. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Pittsburgh allowed the 13th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity and ranked 16th in fantasy points per target versus perimeter wide receivers. Pittsburgh added Jamel Dean this offseason, so I'm expecting them to improve upon last season's stretch run numbers. The only hope for London is that he sees enough volume in Week 1 to outkick Rush's inefficiencies.

Over the last two seasons, Tee Higgins has been the WR13 and WR5 in fantasy points per game. Last season, with Joe Burrow under center in Weeks 14-18, Higgins had an 18.8% target share with 67.8 receiving yards per game, 2.20 yards per route run, a 25.6% first-read share, and 0.106 first downs per route run. Those are all incredibly impressive per-route metrics. For context, if Higgins had kept up that pace for an entire season with Burrow, he would have ranked 12th in receiving yards per game, 19th in yards per route run, 28th in first-read share, and 17th in first downs per route run among wideouts (minimum 200 routes). If this offense doesn't look stuck in the mud for Week 1, Higgins should get off to a nice start against a secondary that allowed the tenth-most yards per target and the 11th-most fantasy points per game to perimeter wide receivers.

injury.comment: Tee Higgins (foot) cleared for Week 1

news.title: Tee Higgins (foot) cleared for Week 1

fp.note: Bucky Irving has dealt with a number of injuries in his short career with a foot sprain and a shoulder/ AC joint sprain last year. Rewinding to 2024, he also dealt with hip, back, toe, and hamstring issues. When he was on the field last year, he averaged 20.3 touches and 86.5 total yards as the RB17 in fantasy points per game. His efficiency suffered massively from the injuries last year after being a wondrous per-touch monster in 2024. Last year, among 49 qualifying backs, he was 43rd in explosive run rate, 35th in missed tackle rate, and 46th in yards after contact per attempt. Those dips are explainable, but they are still concerning for a back that is on the smaller side and has been banged up quite often over the last two seasons. Yes, Rachaad White is gone, but Irving will still have to contend with Kenneth Gainwell in what I'm projecting to be a split backfield. It's tough projecting this matchup with all of the moves the Cincy made this offseason to overhaul their defensive line with the additions of Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, Boye Mafe, and Cashius Howell. I'm treating it as a neutral matchup with the ability to be a positive one for Irving. Last year, Cincy allowed the seventh-highest explosive run rate and rushing success rate and the fourth-most yards before contact per attempt to backs.

Brian Thomas Jr. was one of the biggest busts of the 2025 season. He dealt with a high ankle sprain and a shoulder issue and never looked like the player we all loved during his rookie season. Once Thomas Jr. was "healthy" and Jakobi Meyers was on the roster, Thomas was relegated to a field-stretching role. In Weeks 13-18, he had only two top-24 outings in weekly scoring (WR15, WR23) with a 14.9% target share (18.1 aDOT), 47.8 receiving yards per game, 1.65 yards per route run, three red zone targets, and a 20.6% first-read share. If Thomas Jr. is going to have a bounce-back campaign, I don't think it starts in Week 1. Last year, when Tyson Campbell and Denzel Ward were on the field together as full-time players, the Cleveland pass defense was a shutdown unit against perimeter wide receivers. In their eight games together, the Browns' pass defense allowed only 1.43 fantasy points per target and 7.24 yards per target to perimeter wide receivers. Over the entire season, those would have been the third-lowest marks in each category in the NFL. In that sample, Cleveland was also elite at defending against deep passing, giving up only a 31% completion rate and a 73.1 passer rating. Over the entire season, those would have ranked as sixth-best and seventh-best against deep passing.

injury.comment: Thomas Jr. suffered the apparent shoulder injury in the second quarter of the Week 1 contest, hauling in all three of his targets for 40 yards prior to exiting.

news.title: Brian Thomas Jr. (shoulder) questionable to return

fp.note: Last year, before losing the rest of his season to a torn ACL (Week 9), Tucker Kraft was the TE1 in fantasy points per game. In Weeks 1-8, among 33 qualifying tight ends, Kraft ranked seventh in target share (18.3%), first in receiving yards per game (67), second in yards per route run (2.71), seventh in first-read share (21.6%), and second in first downs per route run (0.121). Kraft was also a YAC gawd, leading all tight ends in yards after the catch per reception and missed tackles forced per reception. We'll see what Kraft's route share and overall snap share are in Week 1. The matchup isn't great for Kraft, but I'm not going to count him out in Week 1. Last year, Minnesota allowed the eighth-fewest yards per target and the 11th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Matthew Stafford had arguably the best season of his NFL career last year, taking down the MVP award. Stafford finished with a career-high passing touchdown rate (7.7%) as the QB4 in fantasy points per game. It was easily his best season since his first year with the Rams, when he was the QB11 in fantasy points per game. Last year, among 38 qualifying quarterbacks, Stafford was seventh-best in yards per attempt and fantasy points per dropback, 25th in adjusted completion rate, second in hero throw rate, and 13th in catchable target rate. Stafford should have time to operate from the pocket this week. Yes, San Francisco will have an improved pass rush with Nick Bosa back (limited to three games last year) and the addition of Osa Odihizuwa, but this is still a defense that had the third-lowest pressure rate and the fewest sacks in the NFL last season. Last year, the 49ers gave up the 11th-most passing touchdowns, the tenth-highest passing success rate, and the tenth-most passing yards. Stafford should have a nice Week 1. Last year, in his two games against the 49ers, he was the QB8 and QB2 in weekly fantasy scoring with at least three passing touchdowns in each game.

Kyle Monangai has some deep league flex appeal for Week 1. Last year, in Weeks 10-18, Monangai led D'Andre Swift with 19 red zone rushing attempts compared to Swift's 18 while producing as the RB33 in fantasy points per game. During the same span, Monangai averaged 12.2 touches and 55.8 total yards while having a 28.8% route share.
